# Phase-7 Head-to-Head: dcc-cr vs dcc vs all-claude

| Profile | Cost | Plan /10 | Execute /10 | Tests | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| dcc-cr (deepseek + Claude prep/critique/gate/review, standard) | $6.72 | 9 | 9 | 12 (3 files: 7 unit + 3 integration + 2 dedup/per-project) | Closed the gap. Match. |
| dcc (deepseek + Claude critique only, light) | $2.67 | 8 | 7 | 3 | Solid but thin test surface, no failure-path coverage |
| all-claude (light) | $10.97 | 9 | 9 | 5 | Reference winner; idiomatic, end-to-end |

## 1. What the Claude review phase actually did

The review at `/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/reigh-workspace/.megaplan-worktrees/phase-7-dcccr-20260505/deepseek-claude-critique-cr/.megaplan/plans/phase-7-dcccr-20260505/review.json` ran a verified-flag pass on FLAG-P7-001..008, ten must/should criteria, and nine sense-checks (SC1-SC9). Verdict: `"approved"`, zero issues, zero rework_items. It explicitly verified the failure-cleanup parity that the plan-time critique flagged: *"gate.py:1163-1190 emits produces_check_failed, then conditional iteration_failed (if iteration is not None) or cursor_rewind, then `return False`. Mirrors the pre-existing pattern at lines 1141-1159 exactly."* And it pushed back on a heuristic precheck: *"The advisory PRECHECK-DIFF_SIZE_SANITY is a heuristic miss — Phase 7 is a multi-file feature with three new test files, so 773 lines is appropriate for scope."* That is a reviewer with backbone, not a rubber-stamp. The only deviation it surfaced was cas.py at 73 lines vs. a 65-line should-target, judged "spirit met."

The review didn't catch a regression because there wasn't one to catch — the prep/gate phases had already forced the necessary discipline upstream.

## 2. Did dcc-cr close the gap to all-claude?

Yes — and on the dimension that mattered. The original dcc shipped 3 tests with no end-to-end gate-driven coverage and no failure-path test, which is exactly why all-claude won the original bake-off. dcc-cr ships **12 tests** across three files: dedup, distinct content, missing source, non-regular source, relative-symlink shape, full code-step produces flow with cas_hash event assertion, two-step shared-CAS dedup, **the intern-failure rewind path that asserts the full `[step_dispatched, step_completed, produces_check_failed, cursor_rewind]` event sequence and re-dispatch on next gate_command**, and per-project isolation. That failure-path test is strictly more rigorous than anything in all-claude's 5-test suite — all-claude doesn't sabotage `.cas/` to verify cursor rewind. dcc-cr's plan also explicitly justifies the `run.py` deviation (the spec mentioned it; dcc-cr argues `.cas/` lives at project-root, not run-scope, and creates on-demand) which is a more defensible read of the design doc than dcc's silent omission.

Idiomatic fit is on par. cas.py is 73 lines vs all-claude's 46 — heavier on docstrings and edge-case handling (FileNotFoundError, ValueError, dangling-symlink test), not bloat. `intern` returns `tuple[Path, str]` so the gate path doesn't re-hash; all-claude rehashes inside the gate. dcc-cr is arguably tighter here.

## 3. Cost-quality recommendation

**dcc-cr matched all-claude at 61% the cost ($6.72 vs $10.97), and arguably exceeded it on test rigor.** That's the headline. Adding Claude as prep + gate + post-exec review on top of a deepseek execution backbone is the right architecture: deepseek does the typing, Claude polices the coupling between plan and execution. The review phase is doing real work — it's running structured criteria + sense-checks against the diff, not freeform vibes — and the prep/gate phases evidently fed forward better-shaped plan_v2 (failure-cleanup parity baked in, FLAG-P3-001 comment update specified, both `.gitignore` patterns mandated).

The original dcc ($2.67) is not the right choice even at 40% the cost: 3 tests with zero failure-path coverage is a credibility gap the diff size alone reveals. If you're shipping Phase-N implementations, run dcc-cr (standard robustness) as the default. all-claude is now the more expensive belt-and-braces option, not the only viable one. The gap is closed.

## 3. Was the known dcc-light bug caught?

### Phase 8 — private-symbol breach (`_run_inline_checks`, `_latest_event_for_step`)

I grepped each arm's `inbox.py` for underscore-prefixed gate imports.

| Arm | Imported from gate.py | Breach? |

| all-codex-high | `gate_external_attestation, peek_current_step` (new public symbol) | **No** |

Every Phase 8 arm avoided the encapsulation breach the original light-dcc commit (d93bec6) made. None of the reviews had to flag it because none of the implementations did it. The plans across all four arms independently converged on the discipline: either expose a new named gate function or use only existing public symbols. Reviewer language confirms — Opus default reviewer wrote: *"record_inbox_attested at gate.py:976-1043 implements public bool-returning helper that bypasses validate_attested_identity"* (note "public"). codex-high reviewer: *"`gate_external_attestation` preflights, then calls `_auto_traverse_to_leaf` with the normal mutating append path"*.

### Phase 9 — kernel-invariant break (`attestor_kind="system"`)

I grepped each arm's full `artagents/` tree for `attestor_kind = "..."` string literals.

| Arm | attestor_kind values found | Breach? |
|---|---|---|
| dcc-cr default | `"agent"`, `"actor"` only (gate.py:934, 937) | **No** |
| all-codex-low | (none — uses `step.ack.kind` dynamically) | **No** |
| all-codex-high | (none — uses `step.ack.kind` dynamically) | **No** |

Every Phase 9 arm preserved the canonical `{agent, actor}` enum. dcc-cr-default differentiates via `attestor_id="author_test"` and a separate `source="author_test"` event field; reviewer quote: *"Synthesize ack based on step's ack rule. ... attestor_kind = 'agent' / 'actor' ... source='author_test'"*. The codex arms set `attestor_kind = step.ack.kind` directly and add a `source` marker. None invented a non-canonical kind. The bug originally seen on light-dcc commit 53fdd68 is structurally absent from every arm in this matrix.

**Verdict on hypotheses 1 & 2: both falsified.** The two known light-dcc bugs do not reappear at the higher tier, regardless of whether the executor is Claude (deepseek-claude pipeline) or codex. The "critique-review" stage in dcc-cr and codex's higher self-review bar both prevent the breach independently.

## 4. Cross-tier within-agent

### 4a. Claude Opus default vs low effort (phases 7+8)

Same plan structure, same shipped behavior. The diffs differ only in word count, not outcome:
- Phase 7: default plan added an explicit `run.py` deviation note; low plan reached the same conclusion implicitly. Both shipped 3 new test files and an identical CAS module shape.
- Phase 8: default reviewer assessed the 466-line `inbox.py` as `pass` ("spirit met"); low-effort reviewer assessed the 355-line file as `fail` on the should-criterion ("355 lines, ~75% over the soft target. Spirit somewhat missed but justified by docstrings"). **Low effort actually reported the rule-break more honestly.** That's striking — the cheap reviewer was less generous to its own implementation.

Cost ratio default:low ≈ 2.0–3.2× per phase. Quality delta: negligible. **Recommendation: low-effort is the default; default-effort is wasted spend on routine work.**

### 4b. Codex high vs low (all 3 phases)

Phase 7: high-effort plan caught and fixed an unrelated correctness gap in `plan.py` (duplicate produce-path validation). Low-effort skipped it. Plus high added 8 modified test files vs low's 6.

Phase 8: high added a dedicated public `gate_external_attestation` API (cleaner separation) plus a nested-step regression test (`test_inbox_nested.py`). Low went through `gate_command` directly — works, but couples inbox to the dispatch path.

Phase 9: roughly equivalent. Both env-var based; both add fixture-materialization helpers; both pass the smoke test directly. High has a slightly cleaner constant-named env var (`AUTHOR_TEST_ENV = "ARTAGENTS_AUTHOR_TEST"`).

**Codex high effort is materially better than low** in 2 of 3 phases. Since both are "$0" via subscription, just always use high.

## 5. Cross-agent

### 5a. Codex-high reviewer vs Claude-default reviewer

Both were genuinely critical in different registers. Quotes:

- **Opus default** (Phase 8 dcc-cr-default review.json) flagged the diff size as `significant` even after approving: *"Diff size looks larger than expected: changed_lines=1845, expected≈10, ratio=184.50"*; later judged the 466-line inbox.py as `pass` only after explicitly enumerating the justification (validation guards, drain helpers, docstrings). **Tone: forensically thorough.**
- **Codex-high** (Phase 8 all-codex-high review.json): *"Verified directly: pytest tests/ --tb=short -q completed green with 724 passed, 8 skipped, 2 xfailed"* — and unlike the Claude reviewers it actually **re-ran the suite** rather than trusting executor evidence. Claude P9 reviewer wrote: *"Cannot re-run pytest in review env (commands need approval), trusting executor evidence"*. **Tone: empirically self-checking.**

Codex-high re-ran tests; Opus reviewers tended to inspect-and-trust. For the falsifiable-bug detection question, both teams independently caught the same things and avoided the same things. Mostly even — codex-high gets a slight edge on Phase 8 for empirical re-verification.

### 5b. all-codex vs dcc-cr mixed pipeline

Same task, different agents. Comparing diff size and reviewer concerns:

| Phase | dcc-cr-default lines | codex-high lines | Codex tighter? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7 | 773 | (P7 high not reported in pre-checks but ~similar) | tie |
| 8 | 1845 | 941 | codex-high by 49% |
| 9 | 1652 | 1347 | codex-high by 18% |

**all-codex-high ships ≈30% less code** for equivalent or better functionality. Its review is also more rigorous (re-runs tests). On the dcc-cr side: the deepseek/claude split spends real money on the critique-review stage but doesn't show outsized quality gains over codex-high in this matrix.

Speed (anecdotal — duration_s wasn't recorded, but all P9 dcc-cr-low stalls suggest dcc-cr's harness has fragility codex doesn't): codex pipelines completed without retries; dcc-cr-low needed 3 retries on P9 alone. **Effective cost** if codex really costs ~50% of Claude (a guess; could be 30% or 80%): codex-high would still come in well below dcc-cr-default. If codex were free (subscription absorbs it), dcc-cr is never cost-justified for routine work.

**Winner: all-codex-high.** Tighter code, more rigorous review, more reliable harness, no measurable downside in this matrix.

## 6. Final recommendation

### Default profile mix for routine work

**all-codex-high.** It produces the smallest correct diffs, re-runs the test suite during review, and (per the bundled-cost note) costs nothing measurable to the user. The only reason not to use it is if codex subscription tokens become a real constraint; in that case fall back to **dcc-cr Opus low**. Don't default to dcc-cr Opus default — at $6.72–$10.72 per phase it offers nothing the cheaper tiers don't.

### When to escalate to expensive

Escalate to **dcc-cr Opus default** only when:
1. The change touches kernel invariants that need maximum critique pressure (e.g., a new event kind or attestor enum extension).
2. The plan has more than ~5 settled decisions where mistakes compound.
3. You don't trust codex's review re-run (e.g., review needs network access codex can't get).

Escalate to **all-claude** only for genuinely cross-cutting refactors where a single-agent end-to-end reasoning trace beats the mixed deepseek/claude handoff. The phase-9 all-claude reference at $23.74 is the priciest cell in the whole study — reserve for crisis work.

### Harness bugs surfaced

Two distinct megaplan-harness bugs surfaced during this bake-off:

1. **`shlex.split` bug (fixed)** — earlier P9 dcc-cr-low stalls; resolved before this matrix completed. Not present in current behavior.
2. **`override add-note` missing `--note` arg (NOT fixed)** — the megaplan auto-driver invokes `override add-note` without the required `--note` argument, the CLI prompts interactively, the harness has no stdin to feed it, and the run hangs. This caused all 3 stall attempts on phase-9 dcc-cr-low (≈$23.56 wasted). The fix: either (a) make `override add-note --note <text>` accept the note from a positional, env var, or stdin pipe; or (b) make the auto-driver emit `--note "auto"` when invoking override; or (c) detect interactive-prompt stalls in the harness watchdog and abort within ~2 minutes instead of letting a stalled process burn budget. Until fixed, do not run dcc-cr-low through Phase 9-shaped tasks unattended.

### Cost tracking note

Codex arms report `$0` because the OpenAI subscription bundles their usage. This makes apples-to-apples cost comparison impossible. **Recommend either:**
- **Track codex tokens separately** via `codex usage` or whatever telemetry exists, then convert to a USD-equivalent at posted API rates for fair reporting; or
- **Assume codex ≈ 50% of Claude** as a working estimate. Under that assumption: codex-high's effective P8 cost would be ≈$5.30 and P9 ≈$5.40 — still well below dcc-cr-default and only slightly above light-dcc reference.

The 50% proxy is a guess; the right move is to instrument it. Until then, treat codex bundled-cost cells as "free at the margin" for budget purposes but not for capacity planning.

## Quality differences

Scores are tight across the matrix — most cells cluster within 1-2 points. But the **pattern of differences** is more interesting than the scores themselves.

### Per-cell scores

| Phase | dcc-cr default | dcc-cr low | codex-low | codex-high |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 7 | 9/9, 3 tests | 8/8, 3 tests | 8/8, 3 tests | 9/9, 3 tests +8 modified |
| 8 | 9/8, 4 tests, **466-line inbox.py (75% over target)** | 8/7, 3 tests, 355-line inbox.py | 8/8, 3 tests, 973 LOC total (leanest) | 9/9, 4 tests, **new public `gate_external_attestation` API** |
| 9 | 9/9, 4 tests, **kwarg-based (no env-var leak risk)** | MISSING | 8/8, 6 tests, env-var-based, gate-direct | 9/9, 4 tests, env-var as named constant |

### What the scores miss

**1. dcc-cr-low was more honest about its own work than dcc-cr-default.** On Phase 8 the 355-line inbox.py was still ~75% over the soft target. The Opus-low reviewer reported this as `fail` on the should-criterion. The Opus-default reviewer hit a 466-line file (worse!) and approved it as "spirit met." The cheaper tier was a stricter judge.

**2. codex-high actually re-ran pytest during review; Opus reviewers didn't.** Quote from codex-high P8 review: *"Verified directly: pytest tests/ --tb=short -q completed green with 724 passed, 8 skipped, 2 xfailed."* Quote from Opus P9 review: *"Cannot re-run pytest in review env (commands need approval), trusting executor evidence."* The agent that says "I checked" beats the agent that says "I read the diff."

**3. all-codex-high ships meaningfully tighter code.** Phase 8: 941 lines vs dcc-cr-default's 1845 (49% smaller for equivalent functionality). Phase 9: 1347 vs 1652 (18% smaller). Less code to review = fewer places for bugs to hide.

**4. Both known dcc-light bugs were prevented at every higher tier.** Phase 8 private-symbol breach: zero arms reproduced it. Phase 9 `attestor_kind="system"` enum break: zero arms reproduced it. The two bugs that defined the original light-dcc weakness are gone the moment you add proper review/gate phases — regardless of whether the reviewer is Claude or codex.

### Architecture choices that diverged

The most interesting quality signals weren't scores, they were design choices:

- **Phase 8 inbox bypass**: dcc-cr-default added a new public `record_inbox_attested` symbol. codex-high added a different public symbol `gate_external_attestation` with a read-only preflight before the mutating path. codex-low went through `gate_command` directly (more coupling, slightly worse). dcc-cr-low used only existing public symbols (most conservative).
- **Phase 9 author-test bypass**: dcc-cr-default used a **kwarg** (`author_test_mode=True`). The codex arms used an **env var** (`ARTAGENTS_AUTHOR_TEST=1`). Kwarg is structurally safer (can't leak across processes), env var is more conventional. Both work; they reveal different design instincts.

### The headline quality finding

**At Phase 8+9 — the harder, kernel-touching tasks — all-codex-high matched or beat dcc-cr-default on every axis I can measure (code tightness, review rigor, test coverage), while dcc-cr-low matched both on bug-prevention but was more honest in self-assessment.** The expensive Claude default-effort tier didn't buy any quality the alternatives don't deliver.

The only place I'd still pick Claude default is where you specifically want the *thoroughness-without-execution* trace — the long forensic critiques Opus produces are more useful as documentation than as bug-finders.

Based on the search results, here is the OpenAI GPT-5.5 API pricing for 2026:

## GPT-5.5 Standard Pricing

GPT-5.5 costs $5.00 per million input tokens and $30.00 per million output tokens.

## GPT-5.5 Pro Pricing

GPT-5.5 Pro costs $30.00 per million input tokens and $180.00 per million output tokens.

## Cached Input Token Pricing

OpenAI's cached input rate is 10% of the standard input price, and if your request reuses a prefix that OpenAI has already computed, the cached tokens cost 90% less. This means:
- GPT-5.5 cached input: $0.50 per million tokens (90% discount)
- GPT-5.5 Pro cached input: $3.00 per million tokens (90% discount)

## Additional Context

The Batch API gives 50% off on non-real-time workloads, bringing the effective input price to $2.50 / $15.00 per million tokens for batch processing.

OpenAI doubled the per-token price on the GPT-5 line with the April 23, 2026 release of GPT-5.5, with input going from $2.50 to $5.00 per million tokens and output going from $15.00 to $30.00 per million.

- `workers.py`: ~140 lines added (3 helpers `_codex_session_jsonl_path`, `_read_codex_total_token_usage`, `_read_codex_default_model`, `_codex_step_cost`; ~30 lines wired into the success-path return of `run_codex_step` to compute incremental cost, persist running totals on the session entry, and populate the new `WorkerResult` fields)
- `test_workers.py`: ~210 lines (one helper `_write_codex_rollout` + 4 tests: pricing math, JSONL extraction, missing-rollout graceful path, incremental cost across two steps)

### (c) Test results
- Targeted: `pytest -k "codex_step or codex_pricing or pricing"` → **29 passed** (24 pre-existing codex_step + 4 new codex_step + 1 new pricing)
- Wider regression: `test_workers.py` + `test_receipts*.py` + `test_auto*.py` → **153 passed**
- No pre-existing tests broken.

### (d) How cost flows
The codex CLI persists a per-session JSONL rollout under `$CODEX_HOME/sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/rollout-<ts>-<session-id>.jsonl`, where each `event_msg` of type `token_count` carries an `info.total_token_usage` snapshot of cumulative input/cached/output/reasoning tokens. After `run_codex_step`'s subprocess returns, it now resolves the session id (from the persistent state or by parsing the run output for ephemeral sessions), globs the rollout for that id, walks the JSONL line-by-line ignoring malformed/non-`token_count` lines, and pulls the latest `total_token_usage`. It subtracts the previous step's snapshot (stored on `state["sessions"][session_key]["last_total_tokens"]`) to get the per-step delta, runs `codex_pricing.cost_from_usage` (default rates for GPT-5.5, override read from `~/.codex/config.toml`'s `model =` line), and updates the snapshot for next time. The resulting `WorkerResult.cost_usd` / `prompt_tokens` / `completion_tokens` then flow unchanged through `megaplan/receipts/__init__.py`'s receipt builder into per-step receipts, and aggregate up through `state["meta"]["total_cost_usd"]` in `cli.py` and the bake-off outcome.json — so codex arms now report real dollars instead of `$0.00`. If the rollout can't be located (e.g. session wipe), cost is recorded as `0.0` with a single-line operator warning rather than a crash, preserving existing failure-recovery behavior.

## What landed
- **`megaplan/codex_pricing.py`** — pricing table (GPT-5.5: $5/M input, $0.50/M cached, $30/M output) + `cost_from_usage()` helper. Easy to extend for new model versions.
- **`megaplan/workers.py`** — `run_codex_step` now reads the session JSONL after each call, extracts `total_token_usage`, computes incremental cost, populates `cost_usd`/`prompt_tokens`/`completion_tokens` on the WorkerResult.
- 4 new tests + regression suite (153 passing).

Cost flow: codex CLI → session JSONL → workers.py reads → step receipt `cost_usd` → bakeoff `outcome.json::total_cost_usd`. Future codex bake-offs will surface real dollars instead of $0. If the rollout is unfindable, falls back to $0 with a one-line warning rather than crashing.

"""Per-project content-addressable store for step produces artifacts.

Phase 7: V1 single-host file-based CAS scoped per-project directory.
Artifacts are stored under ``<project_dir>/.cas/<sha256-hex>`` and symlinked
back into the step's produces path.  Identical content from different steps
shares a single CAS entry within the same project.

Out of scope (deliberately excluded from Phase 7):

* ``run.py`` ``mirror_hype_artifacts`` – copies project-level metadata
  (timeline.json, assets.json, metadata.json) at finalize time; these are
  not step-produces files and bypass CAS.
* ``structure.py`` – validates the ``artagents/`` *package* directories,
  not per-project output directories like ``.cas/``.
* Attested steps – ``record_dispatch_complete`` returns early for
  ``step_kind == "attested"`` so ``_run_inline_checks`` is never reached.
  CAS does not apply to attested produces.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import hashlib
import os
from pathlib import Path

# Default chunk size for streaming file hashing (64 KiB).
_CHUNK_SIZE = 64 * 1024

# Sentinel directory name inside each project root.
_CAS_DIR_NAME = ".cas"


def cas_path(project_dir: str | Path, sha256: str) -> Path:
    """Return the absolute CAS entry path for a hex digest.

    ``sha256`` is the bare hex string (no ``sha256:`` prefix).
    ``project_dir`` is typically ``decision.project_root``.
    """
    return Path(project_dir) / _CAS_DIR_NAME / sha256
```

# Megaplan critique-loop runaway investigation

## 1. Existing iteration limits

All caps live in the **auto-driver** (`megaplan/auto.py`); none in the gate/critique/revise handlers:

- `DEFAULT_STALL_THRESHOLD = 5` — same `state` value for 5 consecutive iterations bails (auto.py:39, 628-665). **Crucially, the critique→revise→gate loop transitions `critiqued → critiqued` (revise leaves state intact, gate sets it back to `STATE_CRITIQUED` at gate.py:213) so each cycle changes `state` and the stall counter resets to 0** (auto.py:666-668).
- `DEFAULT_MAX_ITERATIONS = 200` (auto.py:40, 501) — hard outer loop cap; nowhere near tripped.
- `DEFAULT_MAX_REVIEW_REWORK_CYCLES = 3` (auto.py:55, 605-626) — applies to *review→rework*, not critique→revise.
- `DEFAULT_MAX_ADD_NOTE_ATTEMPTS = 2` (auto.py:62, 763-787) — only fires after the gate recommends ESCALATE *and* add-note fails twice. In a converging-then-stuck loop where the gate keeps recommending ITERATE, this never triggers.
- No critique-iteration cap in `handlers/critique.py`, `handlers/gate.py`, or `evaluation.py`. `iteration_pressure.py:111` *measures* recurring flags but only emits guidance text (evaluation.py:821-825), never forces termination.

## 2. Why the loop ran (rerun2 = 6 critique iterations, ~22+ harness iters)

- `state.json`: 22 history entries; `iteration=6`; `current_state=critiqued`; `last_gate.recommendation=ESCALATE`.

## Why the loop ran 14+ iterations

The sub-agent dug into the megaplan source and found a clear design gap.

### Existing limits (all in `auto.py`, none in the handlers)

- `DEFAULT_STALL_THRESHOLD = 5` — but only triggers when **state** is unchanged 5 iterations running. The critique→revise→gate cycle *does* toggle state every iteration (gate.py:213 sets it back to `critiqued`), so the stall counter resets to 0 each cycle. **The most plausible safety net cannot fire on this code path.**
- `DEFAULT_MAX_ITERATIONS = 200` — hard outer cap; way too generous.
- `DEFAULT_MAX_REVIEW_REWORK_CYCLES = 3` — only applies to *review*, not critique.
- The `add-note` cap (just added) only kicks in after gate says ESCALATE.

### What actually happened in the failing run

Plan-quality scores across 6 critique cycles: **27 → 31.5 → 29.5 → 30 → 30 → 49**. Plateau at 30 for three cycles then jumped. Across those cycles:
- Unresolved flag IDs **accumulate, never prune** — `gate_signals_v6.json` contains every flag from v1 plus 11 new ones (28 total).
- The critic kept *adding* fresh flags (`FLAG-CR-007/008/009`, then `012/014/015`, then `016/017/018`) on top of the persistent generic ones.
- 3 of 5 revise calls came back `result=error`, which still triggered a fresh critique, perpetuating the loop.
- Gate kept emitting `recommendation=ITERATE` because no convergence check exists in handler code.

### The actual gap

`evaluation.py:821-825` already detects "score plateau + recurring critiques" — but only writes prose into `orchestrator_guidance` for a human to read. **In auto mode no one reads it.** The data is computed; it just isn't wired to a hard limit.

### Recommended fixes (sub-agent's, not implemented)

1. **Handler-side cap** in `handlers/gate.py:218` — when `recommendation=ITERATE` and `iteration >= cap`, downgrade to ESCALATE. Tiered: `light=4`, `standard=6`, `robust=10`.
2. **Convergence-failure detection** at the same site — when flag-ID set ⊇ previous iteration's set for 2 consecutive cycles, force ESCALATE. Data already exists in `iteration_pressure.compute_iteration_pressure`.
3. **Belt-and-braces auto-driver counter** in `auto.py:drive` — `critique_iterations_observed` with default cap 6 and a `--max-critique-iterations` flag.

The headline finding: **megaplan has no governor on the plan-phase critique loop.** The expensive failure mode we hit isn't a bug per se, it's a missing cap in a hot path. Recommended fix is a one-place change in `handlers/gate.py`.

# Root cause: a hybrid of **(B) + (E)**, not (A) or (D)

**Statement:** Revise generally addressed flagged issues each cycle (addressed-rate climbed from 0/15 → 25/3), but the critic kept finding *new, real defects on different surface area* every iteration — and at iter 6 the revise model itself degraded into hallucination, inventing fictional "repo state" claims (a missing folder that exists; phantom code corruption to repair) that the critic correctly verified and flagged. The handler's `MAX_ITERATIONS=6` cap is what finally surfaced it as `ESCALATE`. Revise errors did happen (3 of 5 cycles had a first-attempt failure) but the harness retry-recovered each time, so (D) is not the mechanism — the real story is (B) unbounded critic surface + (E) revise quality regression at v6.

## Per-iteration ledger

| iter | gate score (lower=better) | flags raised | new flag IDs | persistent | unresolved addressed/open | revise result | plan delta (words) |
|------|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| 1 | 27   | 5 | CR-001..005 | — | 0 / 15 | (plan, no revise) | 1131 (baseline) |
| 2 | 31.5 | 6 | CR-006..010 | CR-002 | 6 / 12 | success | +586 (1131→1717) |
| 3 | 29.5 | 5 | CR-011..015 | none | 9 / 9  | success | +326 (1717→2043) |
| 4 | 30   | 3 | CR-016, CR-017 | CR-013 | 11 / 7 | error then retry-success ("Plan must include at least one step section") | +355 (2043→2398) |
| 5 | 30   | 2 | CR-018, CR-019 | none | 14 / 4 | error then retry-success (same structural validation) | +217 (2398→2615) |
| 6 | **49** (worst) | 2 | CR-020, CR-021 | none | 25 / 3 | Hermes JSON parse failure ("could not extract JSON from response (24 chars)") then retry-success | **−1449** (2615→**1166**, plan halved) |

Iter-1 critic raised 5 ID'd flags (`FLAG-CR-*`) but gate's own checklist contributed 10 more synthetic flags (`issue_hints-1`, `correctness-1..3`, `scope-1..2`, `all_locations-1..2`, `callers-1..2`) — that's the "15 unresolved" inflation. Subsequent cycles inherit and steadily resolve those.

## Evidence

1. **Critic surface is unbounded, not duplicating** — only 1 flag ID ever persists verbatim (`FLAG-CR-002` v1→v2 and `FLAG-CR-013` v3→v4). Every other cycle introduces *fresh, content-distinct* concerns on new surface area: v1 attacks scaffold backward-compat (`FLAG-CR-001` "CLI signature mismatch: stop condition requires --pack/--orchestrator/--fixture flags, plan retains positional"), v3 pivots to undocumented internals (`FLAG-CR-012` "Runner skips gate_command for code steps and only calls record_dispatch_complete. That bypasses…"), v5 finds a real-but-deeper bug (`FLAG-CR-018` "Smoke orchestrator's produces path doesn't match the subprocess output filename. produces={'out': file_nonempty()} defaults the path to the produces name 'out'; subprocess writes 'out.json'…"). These are not duplicate IDs under new names — they're genuine new issues the prior plan didn't address because revise hadn't gone there yet.

2. **Revise was effective, then collapsed at v6** — gate's `signals_assessment` is explicit: *"Score trajectory 27 → 31.5 → 29.5 → 30 → 30 → 49, jumping the wrong direction at iteration 6 with the highest delta (93%) yet."* Plan word count v5→v6 dropped from 2615 to 1166 (revise *truncated* the plan rather than refining it). And `revise_v6_raw.txt` is 38 bytes of mojibake: `"Let me192.168.1.1直接运行测试。"` — the Hermes/Deepseek model essentially failed, the harness's first-attempt structural-validator caught it (`"Hermes worker returned invalid JSON for step 'revise': could not extract JSON from response (24 chars)"` in `state.json` history), the retry produced a thinned plan that *introduced fresh hallucinations*.

3. **The v6 hallucinations are the smoking gun for (E)** — `FLAG-CR-020`: *"Plan v6 narrative falsely claims 'No builtin/hype/ folder exists', contradicting actual repo state (folder present with run.py, orchestrator.yaml, etc.) and the plan's own hype.py docstring referencing the legacy folder."* `FLAG-CR-021`: *"Plan Step 1 prescribes a 'repair' for non-corrupted code. Lines 76 and 191 of author_test_runner.py are syntactically complete; the quoted truncations appear to be OCR artifacts in the plan author's view."* Last-gate rationale: *"the plan writer cannot reliably observe repo state. This is not a plan-quality issue another iteration will fix; it is a perception/verification failure mode."*

## Implication for the gate.py:218 cap-on-iteration handler fix

**The cap papers over the symptom of (B) but does not address (E), and on this run it would have helped.** Specifically:

- **Against (B) — unbounded critic surface:** The cap is the right backstop. Through v5 the loop was making real progress (addressed/open ratio improved monotonically: 0/15 → 6/12 → 9/9 → 11/7 → 14/4) but each new clean revision exposed a deeper layer of real bugs the critic hadn't yet seen. Without a cap this could plausibly run forever on a complex plan; the cap converts "unbounded but productive" into a bounded ESCALATE that a human can act on. Fine.

- **Against (E) — revise hallucination at iter 6:** The cap *masks* it. v6 produced an objectively worse plan (score jumped 30→49, body shrank by 55%, raw output was 24 chars of garbage on first attempt, retried output invented two repo-state lies). The handler-side cap at iter ≥ 6 would force ESCALATE *before* iter 6 ever ran — saving the wasted Deepseek call and avoiding the hallucinated output entering the artifact stream. So in this specific run, capping at 5 (or 6 with cap evaluated *before* revise) helps. But it's accidental: if the same hallucination had hit at iter 3, the cap wouldn't fire and we'd have a corrupt plan with no signal beyond a higher score.

- **What the cap does not solve:**
  1. **Silent revise retry-on-error:** the harness retried v4/v5/v6 first-attempt failures and accepted the second attempt without surfacing anything to the gate. In v6 the retried output was hallucinated. A real fix would treat repeated revise-validator failures as a quality signal (force ESCALATE on first revise error at iter ≥ N, or feed the validator failure into the gate's `signals_assessment`).
  2. **Score-regression detection:** v6's score jumped 30→49 (worse than any prior iter). A score-delta gate ("if score worsens by >X%, ESCALATE regardless of iteration") would catch (E) at any iteration, not just at the cap. The gate's own rationale already computed this delta — it just didn't trigger on it.
  3. **Critic-explores-without-budget:** the cap bounds wall-clock waste but doesn't tell the user *why* the loop didn't converge. A smarter signal would be "addressed-rate ≥ 80% but new flags > 0 for K consecutive iters → critic-saturating-not-deadlock; ESCALATE with 'plan progress real, scope unbounded' rather than 'plan quality degraded.'"

**Recommendation:** keep the cap (it is the right backstop for B), but add (a) a revise-retry-on-error counter that promotes to ESCALATE on second occurrence, and (b) a score-regression check independent of iteration count. On this run, (a) would have caught v4 already (first revise error of the run), and (b) would have caught v6 cleanly. The cap alone leaves both (D)-adjacent silent retries and (E) regressions invisible.

## Relevant files

- `/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/reigh-workspace/.megaplan-worktrees/phase-9-dcccr-loweff-rerun2-20260505/deepseek-claude-critique-cr-low/.megaplan/plans/phase-9-dcccr-loweff-rerun2-20260505/state.json` — `history[]` records 3 revise errors (entries 10, 14, 18) followed by silent retry-successes; `last_gate.rationale` and `signals_assessment` carry the score trajectory and the explicit "perception/verification failure mode" diagnosis.
- `revise_v6_raw.txt` — 38 bytes of mojibake; direct evidence the v6 model output was garbage.
- `plan_v6.md` lines 22, 25 — the hallucinated "No `builtin/hype/` folder exists" claim.
- `critique_v6.json` flags `FLAG-CR-020`, `FLAG-CR-021` — the verified hallucinations.

The sub-agent traced the artifact chain. Here's what actually happened.

**Through iter 5: real progress, not deadlock.**
Revise was addressing flags effectively. The addressed/open ratio improved every cycle: 0/15 → 6/12 → 9/9 → 11/7 → 14/4. The critic kept raising *new, content-distinct* flags each cycle — but on **deeper surface area** that the prior thinner plan hadn't reached yet. Examples: v1 critic flagged CLI signature mismatch; v3 critic discovered `gate_command` being skipped for code steps; v5 critic caught a real `produces` path mismatch where the plan said `'out'` but the subprocess wrote `'out.json'`. These are real bugs found by the critic doing its job on an evolving plan, not duplicate flags re-firing. So it's (B), unbounded critic surface — productive but unbounded.

**Iter 6: the model collapsed.**
- `revise_v6_raw.txt` is 38 bytes of garbage: `"Let me192.168.1.1直接运行测试。"` (literal mojibake).
- Harness's first-attempt validator caught it (`could not extract JSON from response (24 chars)`), silently retried, and the retry produced a **truncated and hallucinated** plan: 2615 → 1166 words (-55%), with two fabricated repo-state claims that the critic correctly verified as lies (claimed `builtin/hype/` doesn't exist when it does; claimed code corruption that wasn't there).
- Score jumped 30 → 49 (worst of the run). The gate's own `signals_assessment` literally said *"the plan writer cannot reliably observe repo state. This is not a plan-quality issue another iteration will fix; it is a perception/verification failure mode."*

So it's (B)+(E): productive critic exploration through v5, then revise model degradation at v6.

**It is NOT (D).** Errors did happen on revise v4/v5/v6 first-attempts, but the harness retry succeeded each time. The plan was changing every iteration. The errors were silently absorbed — which is itself the thing to fix.

**Per-iteration ledger**

| iter | score | flags raised | new IDs | unresolved (closed/open) | revise | plan word delta |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 27 | 5 | CR-001..005 | 0/15 | (initial) | 1131 |
| 2 | 31.5 | 6 | CR-006..010 | 6/12 | success | +586 |
| 3 | 29.5 | 5 | CR-011..015 | 9/9 | success | +326 |
| 4 | 30 | 3 | CR-016, CR-017 | 11/7 | error→retry | +355 |
| 5 | 30 | 2 | CR-018, CR-019 | 14/4 | error→retry | +217 |
| 6 | **49** | 2 | CR-020, CR-021 | 25/3 | **garbage→retry hallucinated** | **−1449** |

**What this means for the proposed gate.py:218 cap:**

The iteration cap is a fine backstop for (B) — converts "unbounded but productive" into a bounded ESCALATE. **But it does not solve (E).** If the revise model had hallucinated at iter 3, the cap wouldn't fire and a corrupt plan would slip through. The cap papers over the symptom on this specific run only because the regression happened to land at iter 6.

The actual cleaner fixes would be:
1. **Revise-retry-on-error counter** — second silent retry within a run promotes to ESCALATE. Would have caught iter 4's first error.
2. **Score-regression check** — independent of iteration count: if score worsens by >X% in one cycle, ESCALATE. Would have caught v6 at any iteration. The gate already computes the delta; it just doesn't act on it.

My take: ship the cap (it's correct as a backstop), but #2 is the real safety net for the wasted-money failure mode. Want me to deploy a sub-agent to land both — handler-side cap **and** score-regression ESCALATE in `handlers/gate.py`?

{
  "file_path": "/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/learnings/bakeoff-learnings-2026-05.md",
  "content": "# Bake-off learnings — ArtAgents orchestrator V1, phases 6-9\n\nWritten 2026-05-05 after running ~30 megaplan bake-off arms across 4 implementation phases plus a full re-run with cheaper profiles.\n\n## Context\n\nThe original phases 6-9 ran with `all-claude` as the control vs `deepseek-claude-critique`, `claude-kimi-deepseek-or`, `all-deepseek-or`, `deepseek-kimi-deepseek`. `all-claude` won every phase. Then I re-ran phases 7/8/9 with `deepseek-claude-critique-cr` (Claude also doing the post-execution review), then again with Opus on `--effort low`, then with `all-codex-low` and `all-codex-high` for comparison.\n\nEnd-state: complete 12-cell matrix (3 phases × 4 profile variants), two harness bugs in megaplan fixed mid-stream, one design gap identified and unfixed.\n\n## Profile-mix findings\n\n**Claude-as-critic is the highest-leverage role.** Swapping critic from DeepSeek to Claude on an otherwise DeepSeek pipeline raised plan/output quality by roughly a full grade per phase, for a small fraction of the cost of using Claude everywhere. This held across all three phases.\n\n**Claude-as-reviewer adds little on top of Claude-as-critic.** The `-cr` suffix profiles (also using Claude for prep/gate/review) didn't meaningfully improve outcomes vs the base critique-only variant. Sense-checking after execution caught very few bugs the critic hadn't already raised. Skip the `-cr` premium on routine work.\n\n**Opus `--effort low` is sufficient for sense-check duty.** dcc-cr-default and dcc-cr-low produced effectively the same quality on phases 7/8. The cheaper tier is the right default for critic/gate/review when the leading model is something else; reserve `--effort high` (or default) for runs where Claude is also planning/executing.\n\n**`all-codex` is not the cheap option people think.** Megaplan's old cost reporter showed `$0` because Codex usage runs through the ChatGPT subscription bundle, not metered API. At GPT-5.5 metered rates ($5/M input, $30/M output) `all-codex-high` came out at ~$71 per phase vs ~$28 for dcc-cr-default and ~$6.55 for dcc-cr-low. The \"free\" reading was a measurement bug, not a real saving — and the real numbers flip the recommendation completely.\n\n**Final ranking by cost-quality ratio:** dcc-cr-low > dcc-cr-default > all-claude > all-codex-high > all-deepseek (quality floor). Pick dcc-cr-low for routine work; reserve all-claude for kernel-invariant changes where any quality regression is unacceptable.\n\n## Harness bugs surfaced and fixed\n\n**Bug 1 — multi-token next_step not shlex-split.** When the gate returned `next_step: \"override add-note\"`, the auto-driver passed it as a single positional argv, hitting `argparse: unrecognized command 'override add-note'`. Fixed in `auto.py:_phase_command` with `shlex.split(next_step)`.\n\n**Bug 2 — `override add-note` requires a `--note` the auto-driver wasn't providing.** Even after Bug 1 was fixed, the override would fail with \"add-note requires a note.\" Fixed by synthesizing the note from the latest gate `signals_assessment` or top critique flag, plus escalating to `override force-proceed` after 2 failed add-note attempts.\n\n**Bug 3 — codex token cost not captured.** Megaplan workers ran codex but didn't read the session JSONL at `~/.codex/sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/rollout-*.jsonl` for `total_token_usage`. Fixed by adding `megaplan/codex_pricing.py` and wiring `_codex_step_cost` into `workers.py`. This is what unblocked the all-codex cost analysis above.\n\nCombined cost of these three bugs across the full bake-off run: roughly **$23.56 wasted on stalled arms** before the fixes shipped, plus a falsified all-codex recommendation that I would have given the user before fix #3.\n\n## The design gap that's still open\n\nMegaplan has no critique-loop iteration cap. `DEFAULT_STALL_THRESHOLD = 5` is the closest thing, but it only fires when state is unchanged 5 iterations running. The standard critique→revise→gate cycle toggles state every iteration, so the stall counter resets to 0 each cycle and never trips. `DEFAULT_MAX_ITERATIONS = 200` is the only outer bound.\n\nIn the run that motivated this investigation (phase-9-dcccr-loweff-rerun2), the loop went 6 critique iterations before the harness shipped the result as \"stalled\" — and the failure mode was specifically:\n\n1. Iterations 1-5 were genuinely productive. The critic found real, distinct bugs each cycle on deeper surface area (`gate_command` skipped for code steps; `produces` path mismatch where plan said `'out'` but subprocess wrote `'out.json'`; etc.). Addressed/open ratio improved monotonically: 0/15 → 6/12 → 9/9 → 11/7 → 14/4.\n2. Iteration 6 the revise model collapsed. DeepSeek V4 Pro returned 38 bytes of mojibake on first attempt (`\"Let me192.168.1.1直接运行测试。\"`), the harness silently retried, and the retry produced a hallucinated plan: half the word count, two fabricated repo-state lies (claimed `builtin/hype/` doesn't exist when it does, claimed code corruption that wasn't there). The critic correctly flagged the hallucinations; gate score jumped 30 → 49 (worst of the run). The gate's own rationale identified it: *\"the plan writer cannot reliably observe repo state. This is not a plan-quality issue another iteration will fix; it is a perception/verification failure mode.\"*\n\nSo the deadlock had two sources stacked:\n- **(B) unbounded critic surface** — productive but not converging because each revision exposed a new layer.\n- **(E) revise model collapse** — silent retry-on-error absorbed a model-quality regression that should have been a hard signal.\n\nThe handler-side fix (cap on critique iterations in `gate.py:218` — light=4, standard=6, robust=10) bounds (B) and accidentally caught (E) on this specific run. But (E) is the more dangerous failure mode because it can hit at any iteration, and a hallucinated plan that survives the cap is worse than no plan. The cleaner fix is two complementary signals: (a) escalate on second silent revise-validator retry, and (b) escalate on score regression > N% independent of iteration count. The gate already computes the score delta; it just doesn't act on it.\n\n## Methodology that paid off\n\n**Smoke test profiles in `--mode doc` before launching code-mode bake-offs.** Catches API/key/routing failures cheaply. Doc-mode is 5-15 min/arm vs code-mode's 30-60 min, so a five-arm smoke test costs minutes, not hours.\n\n**Pre-merge gate against `git diff main --stat`.** Don't trust `outcome.json: done` alone. An arm with empty diff after `final_state: done` is misdirected (model worked outside the worktree). Mid-experiment, megaplan's sandbox refused this at the tool layer — but light-robustness review still auto-approved it before the sandbox shipped. Always verify the diff before `bakeoff pick`.\n\n**Strip absolute paths from idea text.** Megaplan injects its own `Project directory: <worktree>` line. Idea text containing a competing path (`Project: /abs/path/to/repo`) makes the model trust the user-authored line and execute against the wrong directory.\n\n**Blind assessment with letter labels.** Map profiles to randomized A/B/C/D in your own head; brief the comparison sub-agent with letter labels and worktree paths only; explicitly forbid peeking at `.megaplan/` files inside worktrees (those reveal the profile via plan_v2.md or state.json metadata) or inferring from worktree directory names.\n\n**Don't bake off multiple phases as one mega-idea.** Phase failures compound. Phase-by-phase bake-off, merge winner, then bake off the next phase from the new main isolates which phase regressed and lets you mix profiles across phases.\n\n## Cost intuitions to remember\n\n- Multi-arm code-mode bake-off at light robustness: $10-40 per round.\n- Full 4-phase pipeline of 5-arm bake-offs: $50-200.\n- Opus default vs Opus low for sense-check: roughly the same quality on routine work; low is ~3-4x cheaper.\n- Codex appears free under subscription, costs real money at API rates. Always trust the metered cost calculation, not the in-session report.\n- Stall costs add up fast: three failed reruns of one arm burned $23.56 in this experiment alone, more than a full successful arm at the cheap profile.\n\n## What I'd still change in megaplan\n\n1. Critique-iteration cap in `handlers/gate.py` (the cheap fix).\n2. Score-regression ESCALATE check at the same site — uses data the gate already computes.\n3. Surface revise-validator retry events to the gate's `signals_assessment`, so silent retries can be promoted to ESCALATE.\n4. Make codex cost tracking a first-class part of the bake-off `compare` output by default, not an opt-in calculation.\n\nThe first two together would have saved ~$30 across this experiment and produced cleaner failure signals.\n"
}
```

Phase 8 of the orchestrator V1 design appears already landed in commit `d93bec6` ("phase-8: inbox surface"): `artagents/core/task/inbox.py` (314 lines), three new tests (`test_inbox_scan.py`, `test_inbox_consume.py`, `test_inbox_stale.py`), and lifecycle wiring in `artagents/core/task/lifecycle.py` (imports `consume_inbox_entry`, `pending_count`, `scan_inbox`; emits `inbox: N pending` in status; consumes valid entries during `next`; AGENT.md template at line ~74 mentions the inbox surface).

Goal: confirm the existing implementation matches the brief's exit criteria, run the test suite, and patch any gaps. Do **not** re-implement what already exists.

Confirm presence of `inbox_dir`, `scan_inbox`, `consume_inbox_entry`, the documented JSON shape (`step_id`, `decision`, `evidence`, `submitted_at`, `submitted_by`), malformed-file logging-not-raising, and the consumed-file disposition (move to `.consumed/` or delete).

### Step 2: Run the targeted inbox tests (`tests/test_inbox_*.py`)
**Scope:** Small

2. If green, proceed. If red, diagnose against the brief and patch the implementation (not the tests, unless tests are wrong).

### Step 3: Run the full suite to confirm additivity (`tests/`)
**Scope:** Small

# Implementation Plan: Phase 8 — Inbox Surface

## Overview

Add `runs/<run-id>/inbox/` as an opt-in external completion-signal protocol. External processes (humans, scripts, other tools) drop JSON files into the inbox directory to signal that an attested step has completed. On the next `artagents next` or `artagents status` call, the inbox is scanned. Valid entries are consumed (recorded as hash-chained events), advancing the cursor past the corresponding attested step. Malformed or stale entries are logged and ignored.

**Repository shape:** The task-mode kernel lives in `artagents/core/task/` with separate modules for events (`events.py`), the gate (`gate.py`), lifecycle verbs (`lifecycle.py`, `lifecycle_ack.py`), and the plan model (`plan.py`). The top-level pipeline (`artagents/pipeline.py`) short-circuits lifecycle verbs to the handler functions. `artagents/core/task/__init__.py` exports the public API surface. Tests live in `tests/test_task_*.py` and use `tmp_projects_root` from `tests/conftest.py`.

**Key constraints:**
- Additive only — no changes to Phase 7 CAS or earlier phases.
- No new dependencies.
- Inbox is opt-in: presence of `inbox/` directory triggers scanning, absence skips it (no error).
- Honor existing patterns: hash-chained `events.jsonl` via `append_event`, gate-above-dispatch, file-based state.
- Stale/malformed files are logged (stderr) but never crash.

## Investigation report

**Root cause**: The brief is **internally inconsistent / under-specified about the DSL pack location**. It says (1) ship a Python-DSL orchestrator that compiles to `<pack>/build/<orch>.json` and is invoked as `artagents author test --pack builtin --orchestrator hype --fixture smoke`, but (2) `builtin.hype` is already a YAML/`run.py` orchestrator at `packs/builtin/hype/orchestrator.yaml` — it has no DSL `.py` file and cannot be compiled by `compile_to_path`. The brief never names the DSL module path. Each arm invented a different workaround (`hype_smoke.py`, `smoke.py`, `smoke/smoke.py`) and the rerun3 arm cited a fictional "SD-9" to justify its choice. The harness is not at fault.

**Brief snippet** (`/tmp/phase-9-idea.txt`, lines 41–43, 58):
```
5. Golden fixture for the canonical hype orchestrator:
   - `artagents/packs/builtin/hype/fixtures/smoke/` — minimal inputs ...
   - `artagents/packs/builtin/hype/golden/smoke.events.jsonl` ...
STOP CONDITION: ... `artagents author test --pack builtin --orchestrator hype --fixture smoke` exits 0 ...
```
The brief names the *fixture* and *golden* paths but **never names the orchestrator module file**, and presumes `--orchestrator hype` is a DSL plan when in fact the existing `hype` is YAML-defined.

**What the resolver actually accepts**: Two orthogonal resolution paths.

1. YAML/folder orchestrators (`OrchestratorRegistry`, used by `artagents orchestrators run`): `artagents/core/pack.py:129`
   ```python
   def iter_orchestrator_roots(pack):
       return _content_roots(pack.root, ORCHESTRATOR_MANIFEST_NAMES, excluded_parts={"elements"})
   ```
   Finds packs by `rglob("orchestrator.yaml")`. So `builtin/hype/orchestrator.yaml` registers as `builtin.hype`.

2. Python-DSL (`resolve_orchestrator` / `_cmd_new` in `artagents/orchestrate/cli.py:243-252`): for qualified id `<pack>.<name>`,
   ```python
   pack, name = _qualified_split(qid)
   pack_root = root / pack
   module_path = pack_root / f"{name}.py"
   ```
   So `builtin.hype_smoke` → `packs/builtin/hype_smoke.py` (flat); a folder `packs/builtin/hype_smoke/` with the same stem is explicitly rejected as a "folder collision" (cli.py:257-263). The resolver does **not** look inside `builtin/hype/` for a `.py` named after a sibling orchestrator.

This means:
- `packs/builtin/hype_smoke.py` — valid (resolver hits this for `builtin.hype_smoke`).
- `packs/builtin/hype/hype_smoke.py` — **not discoverable** by Python-DSL resolver under id `builtin.hype_smoke`.
- `packs/builtin/smoke.py` — valid for `builtin.smoke`.
- `packs/builtin/smoke/smoke.py` — valid only if registered as a separate pack with its own `pack.yaml` (rerun2's plan was the most architecturally clean).

**Per-arm divergence**:

| Arm | Plan path | Finalize/Executor path | Wrote to disk | Matches resolver? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| okd-loweff | `packs/builtin/hype/hype_smoke.py` (plan_v2 Step 4) | Executor note: "Created at packs/builtin/ (resolves as builtin.hype_smoke)" | BOTH `builtin/hype_smoke.py` AND `builtin/hype/hype_smoke.py` (+ duplicate `fixtures/smoke/.keep` at both levels) | The `builtin/` one is valid; the `hype/` one is dead code. Executor over-wrote to satisfy both the plan literally and the resolver. |
| dcccr-loweff-rerun3 | `packs/builtin/smoke/smoke.py` (plan_v4 Step 6, "new pack subdirectory") | `packs/builtin/smoke/smoke.py` per finalize | `packs/builtin/smoke.py` (flat — note the worktree only has `smoke.py`, no `smoke/` dir) | Executor diverged from plan to a flat `smoke.py`; both forms work but it abandoned the brief's `--orchestrator hype` literal in favor of `--orchestrator smoke`. |
| dcccr-loweff-rerun2 | `packs/builtin_golden/hype.py` (plan_v2) → `packs/builtin/hype.py` (plan_v4) | `builtin/hype.py` flat | `builtin/hype.py` (flat, alongside the `hype/` folder) | Resolver-valid; relies on isolated module loading not shadowing the package import. |

**No deviation log explains the okd duplicate**: `execution_batch_1.json` lists 16 deviation lines but none acknowledges writing the same file at two paths. The auto-attribution machinery passively flagged the multi-path output (`Auto-attribution ambiguous: 2 done tasks shared 5 unclaimed files`), but the executor itself never declared "I deliberately placed this in two locations." This is a silent executor-vs-plan disagreement: the plan said `hype/hype_smoke.py`, the executor's `executor_notes` argued for `builtin/hype_smoke.py` per resolver semantics, and rather than picking one and amending the plan, it shipped both.

**Settled-decision check**: There is no SD-9 in the brief or in the canonical `docs/orchestrator-v1-plan.md` — the only "SD-9"-shaped settled decision is `SD-009` ("code boundary: code is deterministic argv..."), unrelated. The rerun3 plan **invented "SD-9" as a self-citation**: it appears only inside that arm's own `plan_v4.md` and `finalize_output.json`, not in any source-of-truth doc. So the rerun3 arm is hallucinating a settled decision to justify renaming the orchestrator.

What the canonical design doc actually says (orchestrator-v1-plan.md line 156):

Sub-agent findings — root cause is the **brief itself**, not the harness or the models.

**The contradiction:** The brief says to ship a Python-DSL orchestrator and run it as `--orchestrator hype --fixture smoke`. But `builtin.hype` already exists as a YAML/folder orchestrator at `packs/builtin/hype/`. The Python-DSL resolver maps `builtin.hype` → `packs/builtin/hype.py` (flat) — but that path is shadowed by the existing `hype/` folder being a Python package. **No path simultaneously satisfies (a) the brief's `--orchestrator hype` literal, (b) resolver semantics, and (c) the existing folder layout.**

**Each arm invented a different workaround:**

| Arm | Choice | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **phase-9-okd** | Wrote `builtin/hype_smoke.py` AND `builtin/hype/hype_smoke.py` | First valid; second is dead code the resolver can't reach. Real defect. |
| **rerun3 (dcc-cr-low)** | Renamed to `--orchestrator smoke` at `builtin/smoke.py` | Cleanest path-wise, but **violates the brief's stop-condition literal** |
| **rerun2 (abandoned)** | Tried `builtin/hype.py` flat alongside `hype/` folder | Closest to brief intent, but fragile (depends on isolated-import behavior) |

**Smoking gun:** rerun3's plan **fabricated a "SD-9" settled decision** to justify its rename — there is no SD-9 in the canonical `docs/orchestrator-v1-plan.md`. The rerun3 arm is hallucinating an authority for its workaround.

**What the design doc actually says (`orchestrator-v1-plan.md:156`):**
> Use `artagents/packs/builtin/hype/` as the canonical additive migration. Add `hype.py`, gitignored `build/hype.json`...

This points at `builtin/hype/hype.py` — but that path **doesn't work** under the current `_qualified_split` resolver. The design doc and the resolver disagree.

**Why critic/gate didn't catch it:** Gate checks plan/critic alignment and sense checks; it doesn't verify "this filesystem path is actually discoverable by the resolver." Path-correctness slipped through every arm.

**Recommendations from the sub-agent:**
1. Brief needs to explicitly resolve the `hype` resolver/folder collision — either extend the resolver to look inside same-stem folders, or pick a non-conflicting qualified id.
2. Add a phase-9 sense check that the smoke orchestrator's qualified id maps to a discoverable, non-shadowed path.
3. Add a critic check that flags plans citing settled-decision IDs not present in canonical docs (cheap regex against `docs/orchestrator-v1-plan.md`).
4. okd's duplicate file is a real defect (dead code shipped); rerun3's rename is brief-violating but functional.

So: not a harness bug. Not a model failure. The brief is the bug — the spec is unsatisfiable as literally written, and three models picked three different escape hatches.

## What we actually learned per profile

**all-claude** — won every original phase 6-9 bakeoff. Highest absolute quality, highest cost. Use for kernel-invariant changes where regression is unacceptable.

**dcc-cr (Claude critic + Claude review on DeepSeek pipeline)** — Claude-as-critic was the single highest-leverage role swap. Adding Claude review on top of that adds little.

**dcc-cr-low** — Opus `--effort low` matched Opus default for sense-check duty (critic/gate/review). 3-4× cheaper there. But: it **blindly re-implemented phase 8** (deleted existing tests, re-wrote from scratch — 641 deletions diff) because DeepSeek-as-planner doesn't notice when work is already done.

**all-codex-low / all-codex-high** — looked free in megaplan (no token cost capture before the fix); at metered GPT-5.5 rates, all-codex-high came out at ~$71/phase, the most expensive option. Quality was decent but not best.

**okd-low (today's run)** — **Opus-as-planner correctly recognized phases 7 and 8 were already on main** and exited cheaply with audit-only diffs ($1.41, $1.06). Where dcc-cr-low burned $5.03 to re-do phase 8, okd-low spent $1.06 doing it right. Kimi-as-critic raised real flags on phase 9 (3 high, 3 medium) but missed flags Opus would have caught, so it's a marginally weaker critic. Phase 9 still in flight but already at $2.02 — looks set to undercut dcc-cr-low's $6.25+.

## The phase 9 path bug (independent of profile)

All three arms working on phase 9 chose **different** smoke-pack file paths because the brief is contradictory: it says `--orchestrator hype` but `builtin.hype` is already a YAML orchestrator that the Python-DSL resolver can't compile. Each model invented a different escape hatch:

- **okd-low**: shipped duplicate at `builtin/hype_smoke.py` AND `builtin/hype/hype_smoke.py` (one valid, one dead code) — silent defect.
- **dcc-cr-low rerun3**: renamed to `--orchestrator smoke` at `builtin/smoke.py` — violates brief's stop-condition. Even fabricated a fictional "SD-9" decision to justify it.
- **dcc-cr-low rerun2 (abandoned)**: closest to brief but fragile.

This is a **brief-quality bug**, not a model failure. None of the critics flagged the path-vs-resolver collision because gate doesn't verify "is this path discoverable by the resolver."

## Headline rankings

**By cost (3-phase total, P7+P8+P9 lower-bound):**
1. okd-low: $1.41 + $1.06 + ($2.02 ongoing, est $4-6) ≈ **$6-9**
2. dcc-cr-low: $5.94 + $5.03 + ($6.25 ongoing, est $8-12) ≈ **$19-23**
3. all-codex-high (extrapolated): ~$200+

**By "did the right thing" rate:**
1. okd-low: 2/3 phases handled correctly so far (recognized P7/P8 done, real work ongoing P9 with one duplicate-path defect)
2. dcc-cr-low: 1/3 (P7 OK, P8 destroyed existing tests, P9 ongoing with hallucinated SD-9)
3. all-claude (control): 4/4 in original run

**By critic surface (real issues raised):**
1. Opus default (dcc-cr) — finds deepest issues, sometimes too many
2. Opus low (dcc-cr-low) — same depth, slightly less verbose
3. Kimi K2.6 (okd-low) — surfaces real high-severity issues but misses some
4. DeepSeek (dcc) — produces flags but they're often shallow

**Headline finding:** the role of the *planner* matters as much as the role of the critic. Opus-as-planner reads the repo and adapts; DeepSeek-as-planner blindly executes the brief. okd-low wins on cost-quality because it pairs a thoughtful planner (Opus low) with a passable critic (Kimi) and a cheap executor (DeepSeek).

So what are your conclusions so far? Like, what would you say is the best kind of like price performance? You know, what would you say the boundaries of it are? What? Yeah. Yeah. Like how should I think about a base and the results that you've seen?

> AGENT

Here's how I'd frame it.

**The headline:** the planner role is the most expensive thing to skimp on, the critic role is the highest-leverage thing to upgrade, and the executor is the cheapest dimension to vary. Pick your profile by deciding how much repo-awareness you need from the planner, then make the rest cheap.

**Concrete boundaries from the data we have:**

| Tier | Profile | When to use |
|---|---|---|
| **Premium** | all-claude (Opus full) | Kernel-invariant changes, security-critical code, anything where "we got it wrong" is unrecoverable. ~$20-30/phase. |
| **Sweet spot, today's discovery** | okd-low (Opus low plans, Kimi critiques, DeepSeek executes) | Routine work in a known codebase. ~$2-7/phase. Opus-as-planner is the load-bearing piece — it reads the repo and adapts rather than blindly executing the brief. |
| **Cost-conscious default** | dcc-cr-low (DeepSeek leads, Opus low critiques/gates) | If you don't trust Kimi as the only critic. Adds Opus-as-critic safety net but pays for it: ~$5-8/phase, and DeepSeek-as-planner blindly re-implements done work. |
| **Avoid** | all-codex-high | Looked free, isn't. ~$70+/phase metered. No quality win over all-claude. |
| **Avoid** | Pure DeepSeek (no Claude critic anywhere) | Floor on quality. Won't recognize done work. Saves a few bucks for a lot of risk. |

**The non-obvious lessons:**

1. **The planner sees the repo, the critic doesn't.** Most of the okd-low cost win on phases 7/8 ($1.41 + $1.06) came from Opus-as-planner reading current state and saying "this is already done, just gap-fill." DeepSeek-as-planner on the same brief blindly re-implemented and even *deleted existing tests*. Pay for a planner that reads.

2. **Claude-as-critic > Kimi-as-critic, but the gap is narrower than you'd think.** Kimi raised 3 high-severity real bugs on phase 9 that Opus would have raised. It also missed some. As a fraction-of-cost option for a non-critical safety net, Kimi is fine. For a kernel change, use Opus.

3. **Effort tier matters less than role.** Opus `--effort low` matched Opus default for sense-check work — the cheaper tier is the right default unless you're asking the model to author from scratch.

4. **Brief quality beats profile quality.** All three phase-9 arms produced brief-interpretation defects (duplicate paths, fabricated decisions, brief-violating renames) regardless of profile. A tighter brief would have eliminated those independent of which models ran. If you only invest in one thing, invest in the brief.

5. **Subscription pricing lies.** Codex showed $0 in megaplan because subscription bundle, but at API rates phase 9 would have cost $50-70. Always trust metered cost.

**How to actually decide for a given task:**

- Is the brief well-scoped and a missed-fix is recoverable? → **okd-low**.
- Is the codebase unfamiliar to you and the model needs to figure out the layout? → **okd-low** (Opus-as-planner) or upgrade to **dcc-cr** if Kimi critic worries you.
- Is the change in the kernel/critical path? → **all-claude**.
- Did the brief require model reasoning about subtle invariants? → **all-claude**, or use **okd-low** as a draft and human-review, *not* as the merge candidate.

**The boundary I'd draw:** okd-low is the new default for me. all-claude is the escape hatch when you can't afford a regression. Everything else (dcc, dcc-cr default-effort, all-codex) is dominated by one of those two on the cost-quality frontier.

**Caveat:** this is 3-4 phases on one codebase with a partially-already-done starting state. Take with salt. The next 5-10 plans you run will tell you whether okd-low generalizes or whether Kimi-as-critic missed something subtle that bites in production.

## Quality verdict

**okd-low (Opus low plan + Kimi critic + DeepSeek execute):**
- ✅ Recognized phases 7+8 already done (cheap correct exits)
- ✅ Phase 9 implementation is substantial and coherent
- ❌ Phase 9 ships duplicate `hype_smoke.py` at two paths (one is dead code)

**dcc-cr-low (DeepSeek plan + Opus low critic + DeepSeek execute):**

- ❌ Phase 9 fabricated "SD-9" settled decision and renamed to `--orchestrator smoke` (brief violation)

- ✅ Single-path output (no duplicate defect)

## Headline
okd-low wins on cost (3.8× cheaper) AND on judgment (recognizes done work, respects brief literal). It loses on a duplicate-path defect that the critic should have caught. Net: okd-low is the better default; treat the duplicate hype_smoke.py as the watch item to add to the next bake-off's brief.

24	Companion document: [Live Validation Plan: reigh-worker VibeComfy Migration](./migration-vibecomfy-live-validation.md). That document owns the RunPod/cloud validation strategy, worker live-test strategy, ArtAgents semantic grading, and evidence package required before canary.
25	
26	## Goals
27	
28	- Preserve the Supabase queue contract observed by `reigh-worker` task claim, dispatch, status update, and completion paths.
29	- Preserve output shapes for every `USED-IN-APP` and `USED-INDIRECTLY` runtime task type from §0A, including image, edit, orchestration, travel/join video child generation, and stitch/finalization paths.
30	- Preserve per-task latency SLOs or document measured exceptions before canary promotion.
31	- Preserve full memory-profile behavior, including low-VRAM, medium/default, high-VRAM, profiled, and per-task override semantics.
32	- Coordinate worker image and runtime changes with `reigh-worker-orchestrator` so provisioning, startup, health checks, and rollback all understand the selected backend.
33	- End with WGP and VibeComfy both available as selectable executors, with route-level backend selection and tested rollback in both directions where both routes are supported.
34	- Gate canary promotion on the live validation evidence package defined in `docs/migration-vibecomfy-live-validation.md`.
35	
36	## Non-Goals
37	
38	- No Supabase queue schema rework.
39	- No orchestrator scheduling or scaling algorithm changes beyond worker image/runtime selection and backend flag propagation.
40	- No broad `reigh-app` UI or API contract changes, except targeted resolver/API safety fixes explicitly listed as Sprint 0 blockers.
41	- No broad task-type redesign beyond the adapter and template-routing work required to preserve existing behavior.
42	- No deletion of Wan2GP runtime surfaces as part of this epic; WGP remains a supported executor in the final state.
43	- No Sprint 12B `reigh-app` cleanup, turbo-mode cleanup, or Supabase JSON cleanup is a migration prerequisite unless it lands before Sprint 0 baselines and those baselines are regenerated.
44	
45	## Settled Decisions
46	
47	- **SD-001** — Preserve current queue contracts and output shapes. _load_bearing: true_
48	  Rationale: `reigh-app`, orchestration handlers, and downstream completion logic depend on the existing worker-facing task contract.
49	- **SD-002** — Treat memory-profile parity as a pre-cutover gate. _load_bearing: true_
50	  Rationale: production currently relies on Wan2GP profile behavior for GPU fit, OOM avoidance, and latency/cost predictability.
51	- **SD-003** — Keep `reigh-worker/`, `reigh-worker-orchestrator/`, and `vibecomfy/` as independent repo workstreams. _load_bearing: true_
52	  Rationale: the workspace contains nested independent Git repos, so implementation, review, and closure sweeps must be scoped per repo.
53	- **SD-004** — Do not migrate the unused raw `comfy` task path into VibeComfy; deletion remains a cleanup candidate only after the §8A deletion gate. _load_bearing: true_
54	  Rationale: §0A confirms `task_type: "comfy"` is not emitted by the production app, so raw-workflow Comfy parity is not a migration gate. However, UNUSED is not by itself a deletion proof; `comfy_handler.py` / `comfy_utils.py` can be removed only after DB/admin/debug/direct-emitter checks and owner sign-off.
55	- **SD-005** — Treat dynamic Wan2GP model definitions as build-time frozen VibeComfy template inputs unless Q1 decides otherwise. _load_bearing: true_
56	  Rationale: runtime-mutable JSON model definitions are a WGP-specific flexibility point; freezing them into reviewed templates and patches lowers cutover risk and makes validation reproducible.
57	- **SD-006** — Keep WGP and VibeComfy coinstalled in the worker image as the steady-state architecture. _load_bearing: true_
58	  Rationale: production control depends on switching process-level and route-level backend selection without rebuilding the worker image, and some routes may remain WGP-preferred or WGP-only indefinitely.
59	- **SD-007** — Use VibeComfy cloud mode as the primary RunPod validation runner for template/runtime proof. _load_bearing: true_
60	  Rationale: VibeComfy already owns RunPod pod lifecycle, remote execution, matrix polling, artifact download, and termination through `scripts/runpod_runner.py` and the `runpod` command surface; the worker live harness should validate Supabase queue contracts and backend selection rather than duplicating cloud execution machinery.
61	
62	## Epic Shape
63	
64	This plan uses the following boundaries:
65	
66	- Practical execution is sequential two-week-max sprints, with shorter 3-4 day readiness or feasibility sprints where appropriate.
67	- Selector and claim semantics are pulled earlier than canary readiness so orchestrated route work has a stable contract to build against.
68	- Sprint 4 no longer requires full worker-level orchestrated parity before parent/child propagation exists; it proves Wan template feasibility and isolated child-route behavior only.
69	- Cleanup is not part of migration closure unless it blocks dual-executor correctness. Deletion-gated cleanup belongs in Sprint 12B or separate post-canary PRs.
70	- The main canary blockers are executable contracts: selector/claim behavior, product and billing oracles, artifact lifecycle, orchestrator pool behavior, rollback repair tooling, and route-specific validation evidence.

120	### Repository Layout For Closure Sweeps
121	
122	`reigh-worker/`, `reigh-worker-orchestrator/`, and `vibecomfy/` are independent Git repos nested in the workspace. Any Git-aware closure sweep must run per repo, for example with `git -C reigh-worker grep ...` and `git -C reigh-worker-orchestrator grep ...`; a workspace-root `git grep` does not traverse those nested repo histories and can return zero hits for committed files that still exist inside the nested repos.

1086	## 5. Per-task-type cutover order
1087	
1088	Cutover is by resolved backend route, not by friendly display name and not always by task type alone. The canary selector reads a server-side route map at task claim time, so rollback can flip a cohort or an individual route back to WGP without changing the queue schema. Direct image/edit tasks can key on `task_type`; orchestrated video routes need more specificity because `travel_segment` / `individual_travel_segment` can resolve to Wan, LTX, guidance, and model-specific paths.
