1106	
1107	The selector contract is:
1108	
1109	```text
1110	task claim
1111	  -> derive backend_route:
1112	       direct routes:       (task_type)
1113	       travel/join routes:  (task_type, model_family/model_name, guidance_kind)
1114	  -> read backend_selector[backend_route]
1115	  -> in production: missing selector key => WGP/no-claim, never implicit Comfy
1116	     in local/dev: missing selector key may fall back to process --backend / REIGH_BACKEND
1117	  -> claim only if this worker process/pool is eligible for the selected backend
1118	  -> dispatch through the selected executor
1119	```
1120	
1121	For Cohort E, the parent task's resolved backend route is authoritative for child generation unless a child route is explicitly blocked. That prevents mixed WGP/Comfy orchestration where the parent reports Comfy telemetry while the child is silently submitted to WGP. If the parent resolves to Comfy but a child route is WGP-only, unsupported, or FALL-BACK, the parent fails closed or requeues before creating partial/mixed artifacts. Parent-created child rows must carry a route snapshot (`selected_backend`, selector version, parent route key, and support state) because current child creation is persisted through DB rows, not only through an in-memory queue seam.
1122	
1123	### Selector Control Plane
1124	
1125	The production selector is runtime configuration, not a code PR:
1126	
1127	| Requirement | Contract |
1128	| --- | --- |
1129	| Storage | A server-side config table or config-service namespace readable by workers at claim time, with concrete schema/namespace selected in Sprint 6. Direct tasks read this at claim/execution time. Orchestrated parents also persist the selected backend, selector version, and parent route key into child rows or child params when creating children, so child execution cannot drift if selector config changes mid-orchestration. |
1130	| Key shape | Direct: `(task_type)`. Orchestrated video: `(task_type, model_family/model_name, guidance_kind)` plus optional explicit model id where two model ids share a family but have different template readiness. |
1131	| Defaults | Production selector is an explicit allowlist: missing route key means WGP/no-claim, never implicit Comfy. Local/dev may fall back to process `--backend` / `REIGH_BACKEND` for ergonomics. |
1132	| Launch-time backend | Each worker process starts with exactly one backend. `--backend wgp` processes load WGP only; `--backend comfy` processes load VibeComfy only. |
1133	| Claim-time behavior | Worker derives the route before execution and claims only if its launch-time backend matches the selector. Preferred implementation prevents a process/pool from claiming mismatched tasks. Fallback implementation requeues/fails closed before execution. |
1134	| Propagation | Selector updates must take effect within the rollback SLO. Cache TTL must be short enough to meet the SLO, and workers must expose the selector version they used in logs. |
1135	| Permissions | Only the canary owner/on-call role can promote routes to Comfy; malformed, unauthorized, stale-version, or unsupported route entries fail closed and cannot promote Comfy. |
1136	| Audit | Every selector change records actor, old value, new value, reason, timestamp, affected route keys, selector version, and whether the change was emergency rollback or planned promotion. Audit retention is set before Sprint 7. |
1137	| Emergency override | Canary owner can flip a route or cohort to WGP without merge/deploy. Draft PRs are follow-up durability, not the emergency rollback mechanism. |
1138	| Version guard | Selector entries can require a minimum worker image/runtime version; stale workers that cannot satisfy the selected route do not claim the task. |
1139	| Unreachable selector | Fail closed to the process default only for non-canary local/dev. In production canary, selector unreachability blocks Comfy promotion and should prefer WGP-safe claiming. |
1140	
1141	## 6. Rollback plan
1142	
1143	Rollback remains a permanent operating mode. Every Comfy canary and every steady-state Comfy route is reversible by selector, not by rebuilding an image.
1144	
1145	### Rollback Controls
1146	
1147	| Control | Scope | Required behavior |
1148	| --- | --- | --- |
1149	| `--backend wgp|comfy` | Worker process | Process-level default set by the worker startup command. This should map to `REIGH_BACKEND={wgp|comfy}` internally. |
1150	| `REIGH_BACKEND={wgp|comfy}` | Worker process / local dev | Environment default used by scripts, live tests, and fallback startup paths. |
1151	| `backend_selector` | Server-side route override | Read at task claim time. A present route value overrides the process default. In production, an absent route key means WGP/no-claim, never implicit Comfy; local/dev may fall back to `--backend` / `REIGH_BACKEND`. Direct routes may key on task type; orchestrated video routes key on task type + model/guidance route. |
1152	| Cohort rollback | Server-side selector update | Flip one cohort, individual task type, or model/guidance route back to `wgp` without changing task payloads, queue rows, or Supabase schema. |
1153	| Worker image rollback | Orchestrator deployment | WGP and VibeComfy both remain in the worker image through canary and steady state, so the orchestrator can launch WGP-default workers immediately. |
1154	
1155	The adapter scope for rollback is the same as the adapter scope for migration:
1156	
1157	- Direct-queue seam: `_handle_direct_queue_task` -> `db_task_to_generation_task` -> backend queue submission.
1158	- Nested-handler seam: handlers receiving `context["task_queue"]` and enqueueing child generation tasks.
1159	
1160	If either seam cannot honor `REIGH_BACKEND` and `backend_selector`, the relevant route remains WGP-only.
1161	
1162	### Trigger Conditions
1163	
1164	Rollback triggers are defined by §11 thresholds (single source of truth) and Sprint 0 baselines:
1165	
1166	| Trigger (concrete threshold per §11) | Action |
1167	| --- | --- |
1168	| p95 latency >1.10× WGP baseline for a cohort, sustained 24h | **Auto-rollback:** flip affected `backend_selector` route entries back to `wgp` by runtime config update; keep collecting Comfy shadow data if possible. |
1169	| Error-class spike for OOM (any non-zero rate), model-load, schema-validation, prompt-queue, timeout, or missing-output (>2× baseline rate) | Roll back affected routes first by runtime config update; roll back full cohort if error classes cross task-family boundaries. |
1170	| Output-divergence rate >1% over a 24h window (per-frame pHash p95 breach rate per §11) | **Auto-rollback only when measured through isolated shadow runs** with no completion, billing, upload, or user-visible side effects. Otherwise stop promotion, restore WGP manually if sampled/offline evidence is severe, and add examples to the dual-run corpus. |
1171	| VRAM peak >1.05× WGP profile-1 or profile-3 baseline | Roll back affected memory profile / task family and retune `MemoryProfile.to_session_overrides()`. |
1172	| Parent/child backend mismatch in orchestrated tasks | Roll back affected Cohort E routes immediately by runtime config update; block further promotion until child-task seam tests pass. |
1173	| Worker startup or health-check regression after orchestrator flag changes | Launch workers with `REIGH_BACKEND=wgp` and revert the startup-template change that passed the Comfy default. |
1174	
1175	### In-flight rollback policy
1176	
1177	Selector rollback controls future claims; it does not magically unwind tasks already claimed by Comfy workers. Before Sprint 11 canary, each route cohort must have an in-flight policy:
1178	
1179	| In-flight state when rollback fires | Default policy | Required guard |
1180	| --- | --- | --- |
1181	| Direct task claimed, generation not started | Requeue or fail closed before execution so a WGP worker can reclaim. | Preserve max-attempt/retry class and do not debit twice. |
1182	| Direct task actively generating | Let current backend finish if upload/completion has not diverged and task is below timeout; otherwise cancel/requeue only when the backend can prove no partial upload/completion side effect happened. | Idempotent completion and orphan-artifact cleanup. |
1183	| Orchestrator parent claimed, children not created | Requeue parent for WGP if the route was rolled back before child creation. | No partial child rows. |
1184	| Orchestrator parent created some children | Freeze parent promotion, allow already-created children to finish on their selected backend only if parent/child backend consistency is still valid; otherwise mark parent for manual repair or WGP retry from a clean checkpoint. | Parent/child tracking and duplicate child prevention. |
1185	| Child generation running | Prefer drain current child, then route subsequent children through WGP only after parent policy says mixed outputs are allowed. If mixed outputs are not allowed, block finalization and repair manually. | Explicit mixed-output policy per Cohort E route. |
1186	| Stitch/finalization running | Let stitch/finalization finish if all inputs are already finalized and output contract is backend-neutral. | No duplicate gallery/timeline insertion. |
1187	| Upload completed but `complete_task` pending | Do not retry blindly. Run idempotency guard first; either complete exactly once or orphan-sweep the uploaded artifact before WGP retry. | Completion idempotency and billing/refund parity. |
1188	
1189	### Emergency rollback and durable follow-up
1190	
1191	Each cohort canary in Sprint 7 has two rollback layers:
1192	
1193	1. **Emergency rollback:** runtime selector config flip, no merge/deploy required, used by the automated triggers above.
1194	2. **Durable follow-up:** pre-prepared draft PR, mergeable after the emergency flip, that makes any needed code/config/documentation revert durable.
1195	
1196	| Cohort | Pre-staged rollback PR | Mergeable in |
1197	| --- | --- | --- |
1198	| A (image-only) | Documents and durably codifies selector route revert for Cohort A | < 5 min |
1199	| B (image edits) | Documents and durably codifies selector route revert + Qwen-edit code revert if needed | < 5 min |
1200	| E (orchestrated) | Documents and durably codifies route-level selector revert AND drafts `_handle_via_queue_task` revert to dual-seam | < 10 min (two-PR sequence; second only needed if dispatcher regression) |
1201	
1202	PR ownership: Sprint 11 canary owner (named at Sprint 7 kickoff). Drafts open at Sprint 7 setup; one rebase per week to keep them mergeable.
1203	
1204	`reigh-worker-orchestrator/gpu_orchestrator/runpod/worker_startup.template.sh` must pass the selected backend/profile through the worker startup command during canary and steady state. The dual-stack worker image continues to contain WGP.
1205	
1206	## 7. Telemetry and observability
1207	
1208	Telemetry must let operators compare WGP and VibeComfy runs at the same level of detail during shadow, dual-run, and canary. The goal is not a new observability system; it is a compatibility shim that makes Comfy runs show up in existing heartbeat logs, `system_logs`, and debug-card diagnostics.
1209	
1210	### Required Labels and Fields
1211	
1212	| Field | Applies to | Purpose |
1213	| --- | --- | --- |
1214	| `backend` | All task logs and status updates | Values: `wgp` or `comfy`; required for cohort dashboards and rollback filters. |
1215	| `template_id` | Comfy/VibeComfy runs | VibeComfy ready-template id used by the task. Raw `comfy` workflow routes are not migration scope. |
1216	| `memory_profile` | Both backends | Numeric profile 1-5 plus resolved display name; required for prod profile 1 and dev profile 3 baseline comparison. |
1217	| `vibecomfy.run_id` | VibeComfy runs | `RunResult.run_id` from `vibecomfy/vibecomfy/runtime/session.py:35-42`; attach to start, completion, and failure logs. |
1218	| `comfy.prompt_id` | Comfy prompt submissions | `RunResult.prompt_id`; useful for Comfy history, queue, and prompt failure lookup. |
1219	| `metadata_path` | VibeComfy runs | `RunResult.metadata_path`; attach to debug-card context where present. |
1220	| `log_path` | VibeComfy runs | `RunResult.log_path`; capture into `source/core/log/debug_card.py` and failure diagnostics. |
1221	
1222	### Memory and Runtime Metrics
1223	
1224	The Comfy path must mirror the memory-stat shape currently emitted by WGP output logging in `source/models/wgp/generators/output.py:182-208`. At minimum, each run should log:
1225	
1226	- Host RAM used/available.
1227	- CUDA allocated and reserved VRAM.
1228	- Total CUDA VRAM.
1229	- Selected backend.
1230	- Template id.
1231	- Memory profile 1-5.
1232	- Embedded vs managed-server execution path.
1233	- OOM count and error class when the run fails.
1234	
1235	### Log Translation
1236	
1237	| Source | Existing target | Required translation |
1238	| --- | --- | --- |
1239	| `RunResult.outputs` | Worker completion output path | Normalize to the existing output shape for image, video, and orchestrated child tasks. Raw-Comfy is not migration scope. |
1240	| `RunResult.run_id` | heartbeat logs and `system_logs` | Emit as `vibecomfy.run_id` consistently across start, success, retry, and failure paths. |
1241	| `RunResult.prompt_id` | debug breadcrumbs and Comfy diagnostics | Emit as `comfy.prompt_id`; include in failure and timeout messages. |
1242	| `RunResult.log_path` | `source/core/log/debug_card.py` | Add a debug-card link or path entry so support can inspect Comfy/VibeComfy logs. |
1243	| VibeComfy validation failures | Worker retry/fail classification | Map to schema-validation or template-routing error class, not generic Python failure. |
1244	
1245	Dual-run reports and canary dashboards should group metrics by `task_type`, `backend`, `template_id`, `memory_profile`, error class, and worker image version. Without these labels, rollback decisions will rely on raw exception text and task ids, which is too slow for production canary.
1246	
1247	## 8. Dual-executor steady state
1248	
1249	Sprint 12 is not Wan2GP removal. The desired end state is a dual-executor worker platform where WGP and VibeComfy are both installed, supported, observable, and selectable by runtime route. VibeComfy becomes available for the routes that pass parity and canary gates; WGP remains a first-class executor for fallback, comparison, and any route where it is still the better or only proven backend.

Right — that 1430-line doc has 16 sprints (12 numbered + Sprint 0A/0B/0C/3.5/12B). The "8-9 phases" you're sensing is roughly the major coarse-grained chunks. Let me map profile to sprint and give you a triage rule.

## The profile cheat sheet (smallest to biggest)

| Profile | Cost/sprint estimate | Strengths | Weaknesses | When to use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **dccrmed** (DeepSeek leads, codex sense-checks) | ~$3-8 | Cheap; codex-as-prep recognizes already-done state and steers DeepSeek; survives existing infra | Codex critic is analytical but less repo-savvy | Verification, smoke, runbook authoring, anything where the artifact is mostly text |
| **okd-low** (Opus low plans, Kimi critiques, DeepSeek executes) | ~$5-10 | Opus-as-planner is best at reading existing state; cheap critic | Kimi misses some flags; one path-uncertainty defect on phase-9 | Standard implementation in a known codebase |
| **claude-pr-ckdmed-med** (Opus medium plans+revises, codex gate+review) | ~$15-25 (estimated) | Adds Opus-as-author depth; codex's analytical sense-check is the second pair of eyes | Untested at scale yet (the in-flight phase-9 arm) | Medium-stakes implementation where you want belt-and-braces |
| **all-claude** (Opus default, every phase) | ~$30-60 | Highest absolute quality; won every original phase 6-9 | Most expensive | Kernel-invariant changes, contract definition, anything where regression = production incident |

## Triage rule (the simple version)

Three questions for each sprint, in order:
1. **Will a regression here be visible in production?** → all-claude.
2. **Does the work involve novel code in a critical seam (selector, parent/child propagation, claim contract, memory-profile boundary)?** → all-claude.
3. **Otherwise:** start with okd-low; escalate to claude-pr-ckdmed-med if the brief itself feels ambiguous or the codebase area is unfamiliar.

The trap to avoid: treating "this sprint is long/complex" as "use the biggest model." Sprint length and model power aren't correlated — Sprint 0B is a long sprint of mostly script work that okd-low handles fine. Sprint 6 is the same length but defines the contract that everything else depends on, and a wrong selector schema cascades into Sprint 8/11. Pay for that one.

## Sprint-by-sprint mapping

| Sprint | Risk profile | Recommended | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sprint 0A** Kickoff & contract freeze | Low — discovery, naming, document authoring | **dccrmed** | Almost entirely doc work; DeepSeek-as-author is fine when codex prep sense-checks repo state. Check the `turbo_mode` resolver fix manually. |
| **Sprint 0B** Thresholds & golden corpus | Low — yaml + smoke scripts | **okd-low** | Opus-as-planner reads the existing WGP setup well; output is a config file plus regression fixtures, low complexity. |
| **Sprint 0C** Assets/capacity baseline | Low — infra commands + measurement | **dccrmed** | Mostly orchestrator-side commands and disk-size decisions. Don't burn premium on reading bash scripts. |
| **Sprint 1** Memory-profile MVP | Medium — novel code in vibecomfy | **claude-pr-ckdmed-med** | New 5-tier profile mapping with VRAM/wall-clock validation; Claude-as-author benefits, codex sense-check catches profile-overlay bugs. |
| **Sprint 2** Adapter seam + selector skeleton | **High** — defines a long-lived seam | **all-claude** | This adapter is what every later sprint depends on. Cross-repo, route-derivation logic, the start of the executor abstraction. Do not skimp. |
| **Sprint 3** Dual-run harness | Medium — comparison/oracle script | **okd-low** | Mostly Python harness work; existing patterns to follow. Brief is well-defined. |
| **Sprint 3.5** Wan 2.2 VACE dry run | Low — single experiment | **okd-low** | One template, one comparison, ship a PROCEED/FALL-BACK report. Cheap and short. |
| **Sprint 4** Wan template + single-frame | Medium-high — template authoring is fiddly | **claude-pr-ckdmed-med** | VACE cocktail templates live in `vibecomfy/ready_templates/`. Template syntax errors are caught late. Codex-as-gate catches structural issues. |
| **Sprint 5** Qwen / VLM / LoRA preprocessing parity | Medium — multiple sub-features | **claude-pr-ckdmed-med** | Several preprocessing surfaces, each could byte-drift output. Worth Claude+codex pair. |
| **Sprint 6** Production selector/claim contract | **Highest** — defines runtime config schema | **all-claude** | A bad selector schema is a permanent foot-gun. Worker-claim eligibility logic + cache TTL + version guard → too many concurrency edges to skimp on. |
| **Sprint 7** Orchestrator image + pools + artifacts | **High** — deployment + lifecycle | **all-claude** | Worker image, pool sizing, artifact TTLs, drain/kill policy. Mistakes show up in canary as flapping pools or orphan artifacts. |
| **Sprint 8** Orchestrated route propagation | **High** — parent/child contract | **all-claude** | The "parent says Comfy, child silently runs WGP" failure mode is exactly what you can't afford. The lifecycle contract code is small but load-bearing. |
| **Sprint 9** Control-rail + travel-matrix parity | Medium — many small parity smokes | **claude-pr-ckdmed-med** | Lots of preprocessing variants (Canny, Depth, Pose, Flow), but each is bounded. Premium not warranted unless one specific row blows up. |
| **Sprint 10** Canary readiness integration | Low — dashboards, alerts, runbooks | **dccrmed** | Mostly observability config + runbook prose. Save budget. |
| **Sprint 11** Production canary by cohort | Mixed | **all-claude** for any code change; **dccrmed** for runbook/dashboard updates | Per-flip changes are operational. Code patches that go in mid-canary need premium because there's no rollback iteration. |
| **Sprint 12** Dual-executor hardening | Low — final docs + flip tests | **okd-low** | Documentation + verification. okd-low is good at "audit and gap-fill" mode. |
| **Sprint 12B** Optional cleanup | Low — deletion-gated | **dccrmed** | Cleanup PRs are mechanical once the §8A gate is signed. Cheapest profile that reads the gate criteria correctly. |

## Estimated total cost, with smart triage

| Sprint mix | Cost band |
|---|---|
| dccrmed sprints (0A, 0C, 10, 12B): 4 × $5 | ~$20 |
| okd-low sprints (0B, 3, 3.5, 12): 4 × $7 | ~$28 |
| claude-pr-ckdmed-med sprints (1, 4, 5, 9): 4 × $20 | ~$80 |
| all-claude sprints (2, 6, 7, 8, 11-code): 5 × $45 | ~$225 |
| **Total** | **~$355** |

If you instead used all-claude for every sprint: **~$700-1000.** The triage saves you ~half the cost while keeping premium quality where it matters.

## Two specific notes on this migration

1. **Sprint 6 deserves special care even within all-claude.** The selector schema lives forever — wrong key shape cascades into Sprint 8 and Sprint 11. Consider running it twice: once with all-claude → human review → second pass with all-claude in `--robustness robust` (8 critique checks instead of 4) before merging.

2. **Don't bake-off Sprint 0A.** Bake-off overhead exceeds value for short discovery sprints. Just run dccrmed once; if it produces nonsense, escalate to claude-pr-ckdmed-med.

If you want, I can stage the megaplan launches (one sprint at a time, merging winners into main between sprints — that's what this experiment validated as the right pattern, vs. baking all sprints at once).

{
  "file_path": "/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/learnings/profile-selection-2026-05.md",
  "content": "# Profile selection — picking models per phase, with effort tiers\n\nDistilled from the May 2026 ArtAgents bake-off (~30 multi-arm runs across 4 implementation phases plus a re-run with cheaper profiles). The point of this doc is to pick the right profile and the right effort tier for the work in front of you, not to default to the most expensive thing.\n\n## The premium-model question (Claude Opus vs GPT-5.5)\n\nBoth Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.5 are premium models. They are not interchangeable across roles; the experiment found a clear split:\n\n- **Opus reads code and existing repo state better.** When pointed at \"implement phase 8\" on a repo where phase 8 was already on `main`, Opus-as-planner wrote *\"This is already landed at commit X — audit and gap-fill only\"* and exited cheaply. DeepSeek-as-planner blindly re-implemented and deleted the existing tests. Codex-as-planner hit `worker_blocked` from internal sense-check failures and `awaiting_human` gating. Repo awareness is Opus's load-bearing trait.\n- **Both Opus and GPT-5.5 are strong critics, in different ways.** Opus surfaces deep, content-distinct flags (e.g., \"this driver passes hardcoded `'next'` instead of peeking the cursor\"). GPT-5.5 is more analytical, catches structural/contract issues, and as critic+gate it actually steers a DeepSeek planner to read the repo before writing. The single highest-leverage role swap in the experiment was upgrading the critic from cheap to premium; it raised plan/output quality by roughly a full grade.\n- **Don't pay premium for execute.** DeepSeek V4 Pro as the executor is fine. The model writing `for x in y:` doesn't need the same depth as the one reasoning about a contract.\n- **Subscription pricing lies.** GPT-5.5 looked $0/arm under the codex CLI subscription bundle. At metered rates it's $5/M input / $30/M output, and an `all-codex-high` arm came out at ~$71/phase — more expensive than `all-claude` for less quality. Always compute metered cost when comparing.\n\nSo \"premium\" is a misleading singular noun. Match the model's strength to the phase: Opus for plan/author, either premium for critique/gate, cheap models for prep/finalize/execute.\n\n## Effort tier is its own dial\n\nBoth Claude (`claude:low|medium|high|xhigh|max`) and Codex (`codex:minimal|low|medium|high`) accept reasoning-effort tiers. This adds a third axis on top of model and role:\n\n| Phase | Effort needed | Notes |\n|---|---|---|\n| **plan** | medium-to-high | Authoring is where effort earns its keep. Bump to `high` when the codebase is unfamiliar or the brief is long. Stay at `medium` for routine work. |\n| **revise** | medium-to-high | Same as plan — author-side. Pair with whatever you used for plan. |\n| **critique** | low-to-medium | Critique is recognition, not generation. `low` is usually enough for sense-check critique. `medium` if you suspect deep structural issues. |\n| **gate** | low | Gate makes a single iterate/proceed decision from existing artifacts. `low` is sufficient — the experiment showed `claude:low` and `claude:default` produced identical gate verdicts. |\n| **review** | low | Same logic as gate. |\n| **prep** | low | Repository inspection. `low` is fine. |\n| **finalize / execute** | minimal-to-low | Mechanical translation from plan to tasks, then mechanical task execution. Don't pay for reasoning here. |\n\nThe general rule: **author-side phases (plan, revise) consume effort productively; sense-check phases (prep, critique, gate, review) plateau at `low` or `medium`.** A `claude:high` planner with a `claude:low` critic is usually the right asymmetry, not `claude:medium` everywhere.\n\n## System-wide profiles available now\n\nThese all live in `~/.config/megaplan/profiles.toml` and resolve from any project. The first column is what to reach for first; escalate up the table as stakes rise.\n\n| Profile | Roles | Cost band | When to use |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| `deepseek-codex-critique-cr-med` (dccrmed) | DeepSeek leads + executes; **codex:medium** does prep/critique/gate/review; codex-as-prep effectively steers DeepSeek to read the repo. | ~$1-3/arm | Verification, smoke tests, runbook authoring, doc-mode plans, anything where the artifact is mostly text. Cheapest viable profile. |\n| `codex-kimi-deepseek-med` (ckdmed) | **Codex:medium** plans/revises/gates/reviews; Kimi K2.6 critiques; DeepSeek executes. | ~$2-5/arm | When you want codex-as-author rather than codex-as-critic. Caveat: codex-as-planner hit blocking/human-gating failures on phases requiring repo state awareness. Good for greenfield, less good for \"where does this fit in the existing code.\" |\n| `opus-kimi-deepseek-low` (okd-low) | **Opus 4.7 `--effort low`** plans/revises/gates/reviews; Kimi K2.6 critiques; DeepSeek executes. | ~$1-5/arm | The cost-quality winner from the experiment. Opus-as-planner reads the repo and adapts (recognises already-done state), Kimi critic is good-enough, DeepSeek executes cheap. Default for routine implementation work. |\n| `claude-pr-ckdmed-med` | **Opus 4.7 `--effort medium`** plans+revises; **codex:medium** gates+reviews; Kimi critiques; DeepSeek executes. | ~$10-25/arm (estimate) | Belt-and-braces: pairs Opus authoring depth with codex's analytical post-iteration check. Use for medium-stakes implementation. Bump claude effort to `high` for hard plans. |\n| `all-claude` (built-in) | Opus 4.7 default everywhere. | ~$30-60/arm | Highest absolute quality. Reserve for kernel-invariant changes, contract definition (e.g., a selector schema or a wire format), anything where regression = production incident. |\n| `all-codex` (built-in) | Codex everywhere at default effort. | metered ~$50-70/arm | Mostly a baseline for comparison. The experiment found this expensive without quality wins over `all-claude`. Avoid as a default. |\n| `deepseek-claude-critique` (built-in) | DeepSeek leads + executes; Claude critiques. | ~$5-8/arm | Older predecessor of dcc-cr-low. Kept because Claude-as-only-critic on a DeepSeek pipeline was the original \"swap one role, get a full grade better\" finding. |\n| `claude-kimi-deepseek` (built-in) | Claude leads everywhere except critique (Kimi) and execute (DeepSeek). | ~$15-30/arm | Older predecessor of okd-low. Use okd-low instead unless you need Claude default-effort. |\n\n**Effort variants:** the named profiles above pick a default effort tier in their suffix (`-low`, `-med`). For a complex plan, you usually don't need a separate profile — pass `--phase-model plan=claude:high` on the CLI to bump just the authoring tier on top of an existing profile.\n\n## The three-question triage\n\n1. **Will a regression be visible in production?** → `all-claude`.\n2. **Does the work involve a long-lived contract or seam (wire format, schema, claim contract, parent/child propagation)?** → `all-claude`, possibly with `--robustness robust` (8 critique checks instead of 4).\n3. **Otherwise**, start with `okd-low`. Escalate to `claude-pr-ckdmed-med` if the brief itself is ambiguous or you're working in unfamiliar code. Drop to `dccrmed` for verification, smoke, and doc-mode work.\n\nThe trap to avoid: treating \"this sprint is long/complex\" as \"use the biggest model.\" Sprint length and model power aren't correlated — a long sprint of mechanical script work is fine for `okd-low`. A short sprint defining a permanent schema is what `all-claude` is for.\n\n## What dominated outcomes more than profile choice\n\nTwo findings that recur regardless of profile:\n\n- **The brief is the dominant variable.** All three phase-9 arms in the experiment produced brief-interpretation defects (duplicate file paths, fabricated settled-decisions, brief-violating renames) regardless of profile. Tightening the brief beats picking a better profile. If you only invest in one thing, invest in the brief.\n- **Premium-as-planner > premium-as-everywhere.** The single biggest cost-quality win was placing one premium model in the planner role and letting cheap models handle the rest. `okd-low` (Opus low only at plan/revise/gate/review, with most other roles cheap) hit ~3-4x cheaper than `dcc-cr-low` (Claude in critic role only, DeepSeek planning) and produced higher-quality outputs because the planner read the repo correctly.\n\n## Inputs that produced these findings\n\n- 4 implementation phases (orchestrator V1 phases 6-9 in ArtAgents), each ~1-2 days of human work, each with a written brief in `/tmp/phase-N-idea.txt`.\n- 7 distinct profiles tested across the phases at light robustness (`plan → critique → revise → finalize → execute`):\n  - `all-claude` (control)\n  - `deepseek-claude-critique` and `deepseek-claude-critique-cr` (DeepSeek-led with Claude critic, with/without claude review)\n  - `deepseek-claude-critique-cr-low` (Opus low for sense-check)\n  - `all-codex-low` and `all-codex-high` (effort tier comparison on a single-agent pipeline)\n  - `opus-kimi-deepseek-low` (Opus-as-planner, novel)\n  - `codex-kimi-deepseek-med` and `deepseek-codex-critique-cr-med` (codex variants, novel)\n  - `claude-pr-ckdmed-med` (Claude author + codex sense-check, novel)\n- Per-arm metered cost computed from session JSONLs (a megaplan harness fix that surfaced ~$70/arm hidden codex cost the subscription bundle was masking).\n- Quality verdicts via blind A/B/C/D sub-agent assessment plus a pre-merge `git diff main --stat` gate to catch misdirected/empty-diff arms.\n\n## What this doc deliberately does not say\n\n- \"Always use Claude\" — wrong. Codex-as-prep+critic+gate (dccrmed) was a pleasant surprise; it steers DeepSeek planners well and is the cheapest viable profile.\n- \"All-codex is free\" — wrong. Subscription pricing is real, metered cost is what matters when you're comparing.\n- \"Higher effort always helps\" — wrong. Effort plateaus on sense-check duty; spend it on author-side phases.\n"

Use okd-low instead unless you need Claude default-effort. |\n\n## The three-question triage\n\n1. **Will a regression be visible in production?** → `all-claude` or `all-codex`.\n2. **Does the work involve a long-lived contract or seam (wire format, schema, claim contract, parent/child propagation)?** → `all-claude` or `all-codex`, possibly with `--robustness robust` for extremely complex projects.\n3. **Otherwise**, start with `okd-low`. Escalate to `claude-pr-ckdmed-med` if the brief itself is ambiguous or you're working in unfamiliar code. Drop to `dccrmed` for verification, smoke, and doc-mode work.\n\nThe trap to avoid: treating \"this sprint is long\" as \"use the biggest model.\" Length and model power aren't correlated — a long sprint of mechanical script work is fine for `okd-low`. A short sprint defining a permanent schema is what `all-claude`/`all-codex` is for.\n\n## Thinking strength — its own dial\n\nBoth Claude and Codex accept a **thinking-strength tier** that's independent of which model you pick. It's spelled out in the agent spec after a colon:\n\n- Claude: `claude:low`, `claude:medium`, `claude:high`, `claude:xhigh`, `claude:max`.\n- Codex: `codex:minimal`, `codex:low`, `codex:medium`, `codex:high`.\n\nThe tier is the third axis on top of model and role. The principle: **author-side phases (plan, revise) reward higher thinking strength; sense-check phases (prep, critique, gate, review) plateau at low or medium.**\n\n| Phase | Recommended strength | Why |\n|---|---|---|\n| **plan** | medium-to-high | Authoring is where thinking earns its keep. Bump to `high` when the codebase is unfamiliar or the brief is long. Stay at `medium` for routine work. Use `xhigh`/`max` only for genuinely novel architectural plans. |\n| **revise** | medium-to-high | Same as plan — author-side. Pair with whatever you used for plan. |\n| **critique** | low-to-medium | Critique is recognition, not generation. `low` is usually enough; `medium` if you suspect deep structural issues. |\n| **gate** | low | Gate makes a single iterate/proceed decision from existing artifacts. `low` is sufficient — the experiment showed `claude:low` and `claude:default` produced identical gate verdicts on the same plans. |\n| **review** | low | Same logic as gate. |\n| **prep** | low | Repository inspection. `low` is fine. |\n| **finalize / execute** | minimal-to-low | Mechanical translation from plan to tasks, then mechanical task execution. Don't pay for thinking here. |\n\nThe general rule: a **`claude:high` planner with a `claude:low` critic is the right asymmetry**, not `claude:medium` everywhere. Same for codex — `codex:high` plan + `codex:low` gate beats `codex:medium` everywhere on cost and matches it on quality.\n\nYou usually don't need a separate profile per tier — pass `--phase-model plan=claude:high` on the CLI to bump just the authoring tier on top of an existing profile. Reserve named `-low` / `-med` / `-high` profile variants for tiers you reach for repeatedly.\n\n## How Opus and GPT-5.5 differ in our data\n\nWhen stakes warrant a premium model, both are good. They behave differently on different roles:\n\n- **Opus reads existing repo state better as a planner.** Pointed at \"implement phase 8\" on a repo where phase 8 was already on `main`, Opus-as-planner wrote *\"This is already landed at commit X — audit and gap-fill only\"* and exited cheaply. Codex-as-planner re-implemented or hit `worker_blocked` from internal sense-check failures and `awaiting_human` gating. So when the planner needs to figure out where new work fits in existing code, Opus is the safer choice.\n- **Both are strong critics, in different ways.** Opus surfaces deep, content-distinct flags (\"this driver passes hardcoded `'next'` instead of peeking the cursor\"). Codex is more analytical and catches structural/contract issues; codex-as-critic+gate also steers DeepSeek planners to read the repo before writing. The single highest-leverage role swap in the experiment was upgrading the critic from cheap to premium — independent of which premium.\n- **Both are overkill as executors.** DeepSeek V4 Pro as the executor is fine. The model writing `for x in y:` doesn't need the same depth as the one reasoning about a contract.\n\nPick between `all-claude` and `all-codex` (or between `okd-low`-style Opus-led and `ckdmed`-style codex-led mixes) based on what the user prefers, what credits are available, and which model has done better on similar work in this codebase. There's no universal answer.\n\n## What dominated outcomes more than profile choice\n\nTwo findings that recur regardless of profile:\n\n- **The brief is the dominant variable.** All three phase-9 arms in the experiment produced brief-interpretation defects (duplicate file paths, fabricated settled-decisions, brief-violating renames) regardless of profile. Tightening the brief beats picking a better profile. Strength plateaus on sense-check duty; spend it on author-side phases.\n- **\"Profile choice dominates outcome.\"** Mostly wrong. Brief quality dominates. Refine it after every meaningful bake-off — the entries below should keep shrinking and sharpening, not growing.\n\nThe point: pick the right profile and the right thinking strength for the work in front of you. Default to the cheapest tier that still produces correct output, and only escalate when stakes warrant.\n\n## The profiles\n\nThese all live in `~/.config/megaplan/profiles.toml` and resolve from any project. Default to the highest row that fits the task; escalate down only when stakes demand.\n\n| Profile | Roles | Cost band (per phase) | When to use |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| **`nancy`** *(light, quick)* | DeepSeek leads + executes; codex:medium does prep/critique/gate/review. Codex-as-prep effectively steers DeepSeek to read the repo first. | ~$1-3 | Verification, smoke tests, runbook authoring, doc-mode plans, anything where the artifact is mostly text. Default for routine implementation work. |\n| **`holmes`** *(meticulous master)* | Opus 4.7 `--effort medium` plans+revises; codex:medium gates+reviews; Kimi K2.6 critiques; DeepSeek executes. | ~$10-25 | Belt-and-braces: pairs Opus authoring depth with codex's analytical post-iteration check. Use for medium-stakes implementation. |\n| **`all-claude`** *or* **`all-codex`** | One premium model across every phase. `all-claude` uses Opus 4.7; `all-codex` uses GPT-5.5. | ~$30-70 | Highest absolute quality. Reserve for kernel-invariant changes, contract definition (a selector schema, a wire format), anything where regression = production incident. Pick `all-claude` or `all-codex` based on user preference, credits available, or whichever model has done better on similar work. **Possibly with `--robustness robust`** (8 critique checks instead of 4) for extremely complex projects. |\n\nThe names: `nancy` is Nancy Drew (sharp-eyed light-touch detective), `marlowe` is Philip Marlowe (hard-boiled gumshoe who gets the job done day after day), `holmes` is Sherlock Holmes (meticulous master who leaves nothing to chance). Map the personality to the work and you'll pick the right one.\n\n## Three-question triage\n\n1. **Will a regression be visible in production?** → `all-claude` or `all-codex`.\n2. **Does the work involve a long-lived contract or seam (wire format, schema, claim contract, parent/child propagation)?** → `all-claude` or `all-codex`, possibly with `--robustness robust` for extremely complex projects.\n3. **Otherwise**, start with `marlowe`. Escalate to `holmes` if the brief itself is ambiguous or you're working in unfamiliar code. Drop to `nancy` for verification, smoke, and doc-mode work.\n\nThe trap to avoid: treating \"this sprint is long\" as \"use the biggest model.\" Length and model power aren't correlated — a long sprint of mechanical script work is fine for `marlowe`. A short sprint defining a permanent schema is what `all-claude` / `all-codex` is for.\n\n## Thinking strength — its own dial\n\nBoth Claude and Codex accept a thinking-strength tier that's independent of which model you pick. It's spelled out in the agent spec after a colon:\n\n- Claude: `claude:low`, `claude:medium`, `claude:high`, `claude:xhigh`, `claude:max`.\n- Codex: `codex:minimal`, `codex:low`, `codex:medium`, `codex:high`.\n\nThe tier is the third axis on top of model and role. The principle: **author-side phases (plan, revise) reward higher thinking strength; sense-check phases (prep, critique, gate, review) plateau at low or medium.**\n\n| Phase | Recommended strength | Why |\n|---|---|---|\n| **plan** | medium-to-high | Authoring is where thinking earns its keep. Bump to `high` when the codebase is unfamiliar or the brief is long. Stay at `medium` for routine work. Use `xhigh` / `max` only for genuinely novel architectural plans. |\n| **revise** | medium-to-high | Same as plan — author-side. Pair with whatever you used for plan. |\n| **critique** | low-to-medium | Critique is recognition, not generation. `low` is usually enough; `medium` if you suspect deep structural issues. |\n| **gate** | low | Gate makes a single iterate/proceed decision from existing artifacts. `low` is sufficient — the experiment showed `claude:low` and `claude` default produced identical gate verdicts on the same plans. |\n| **review** | low | Same logic as gate. |\n| **prep** | low | Repository inspection. `low` is fine. |\n| **finalize / execute** | minimal-to-low | Mechanical translation from plan to tasks, then mechanical task execution. Don't pay for thinking here. |\n\nThe general rule: a **`claude:high` planner with a `claude:low` critic is the right asymmetry**, not `claude:medium` everywhere. Same for codex — `codex:high` plan + `codex:low` gate beats `codex:medium` everywhere on cost and matches it on quality.\n\nYou usually don't need a separate profile per tier — pass `--phase-model plan=claude:high` on the CLI to bump just the authoring tier on top of an existing profile. Reserve named profile variants for tiers you reach for repeatedly.\n\n## How Opus and GPT-5.5 differ in our data\n\nWhen stakes warrant a premium model, both are good. They behave differently on different roles:\n\n- **Opus reads existing repo state better as a planner.** Pointed at \"implement phase 8\" on a repo where phase 8 was already on `main`, Opus-as-planner wrote *\"This is already landed at commit X — audit and gap-fill only\"* and exited cheaply. Codex-as-planner re-implemented or hit `worker_blocked` from internal sense-check failures and `awaiting_human` gating. So when the planner needs to figure out where new work fits in existing code, Opus is the safer choice.\n- **Both are strong critics, in different ways.** Opus surfaces deep, content-distinct flags. Codex is more analytical and catches structural/contract issues; codex-as-critic+gate also steers DeepSeek planners to read the repo before writing. The single highest-leverage role swap in the experiment was upgrading the critic from cheap to premium — independent of which premium.\n- **Both are overkill as executors.** DeepSeek V4 Pro as the executor is fine.\n\nPick between `all-claude` and `all-codex` based on user preference, credits available, and which model has done better on similar work in this codebase. There's no universal answer.\n\n## What dominates outcomes more than profile choice\n\n- **The brief is the dominant variable.** All three phase-9 arms in the experiment produced brief-interpretation defects (duplicate file paths, fabricated settled-decisions, brief-violating renames) regardless of profile. Tightening the brief beats picking a better profile. If you only invest in one thing, invest in the brief.\n- **One premium model in the planner role, cheap models elsewhere, beats premium everywhere.** The single biggest cost-quality win was concentrating the premium model in author-side phases. `marlowe` (premium only at plan/revise/gate/review) hit ~3-4x cheaper than the all-Claude variants and produced higher-quality outputs because the planner read the repo correctly.\n\n## Anti-patterns to avoid\n\n- **\"Always use Claude.\"** Wrong. Codex-as-prep+critic+gate (`nancy`) was a pleasant surprise — it steers DeepSeek planners well and is the cheapest viable profile.\n- **\"Higher thinking strength always helps.\"** Wrong. Strength plateaus on sense-check duty; spend it on author-side phases.\n- **\"Profile choice dominates outcome.\"** Mostly wrong. Brief quality dominates. If three profiles all produce brief-interpretation defects, fix the brief.\n\n## Inputs that produced these findings\n\n4 implementation phases (orchestrator V1 phases 6-9 in ArtAgents), each with a written brief in `/tmp/phase-N-idea.txt`. ~30 multi-arm bake-offs across 7 distinct profile mixes at light robustness. Per-arm metered cost from session JSONLs. Quality verdicts via blind A/B/C/D sub-agent assessment plus a pre-merge `git diff main --stat` gate.\n"

The plan itself needs rigorous debate. |\n| `superrobust` | robust + parallel review. | Rarely needed. Use when both deep critique and concurrent review matter and you can absorb the parallelism cost. |\n\nThe three dials are independent — pick all three:\n\n| Combination | Use case |\n|---|---|\n| `marlowe` + `light` | Cheap routine implementation, default for daily work |\n| `marlowe` + `standard` | Routine work where you want full sense-check (prep, gate, review) |\n| `holmes` + `standard` | Medium-stakes work with full sense-check |\n| `all-claude` *or* `all-codex` + `robust` | The \"extremely complex project\" combination — premium model AND extra critique checks |\n| Any profile + thinking-strength bumped via `--phase-model` | Tune one phase up without changing the profile |\n\nMost of our experiments were at `light` robustness because we were comparing profiles head-to-head; the cost bands in the profile table above reflect that. Stepping up to `standard` adds prep + gate + review phases; `robust` doubles the critique checks. With the three-dial framework, here's the per-sprint recommendation. Format: profile + robustness + any thinking-strength override.

| Sprint | Profile | Robustness | Thinking strength | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **0A** Kickoff & contract freeze | `nancy` | `light` | defaults | Discovery + naming + contract skeleton. Mostly doc work. Verify the `turbo_mode` resolver fix manually. |
| **0B** Thresholds & golden corpus | `marlowe` | `light` | defaults | YAML + smoke scripts; existing patterns to follow. |
| **0C** Assets/capacity baseline | `nancy` | `light` | defaults | Orchestrator-side commands + disk measurement. Don't pay premium to read bash. |
| **1** Memory-profile MVP | `holmes` | `standard` | `--phase-model plan=claude:high` | Novel 5-tier mapping. Bump plan effort because this is unfamiliar territory; codex gate catches profile-overlay bugs. |
| **2** Adapter seam + selector skeleton | **`all-claude` or `all-codex`** | `standard` | `--phase-model plan=claude:high revise=claude:high` | Defines the executor abstraction every later sprint depends on. Don't skimp. Pick claude or codex per credits/preference. |
| **3** Dual-run harness | `marlowe` | `standard` | defaults | Comparison/oracle script. Want gate + review since the harness will be relied on by every later sprint. |
| **3.5** Wan 2.2 VACE dry run | `marlowe` | `light` | defaults | Single experiment, ship a PROCEED/FALL-BACK report. Cheap and short. |
| **4** Wan template + single-frame | `holmes` | `standard` | defaults | Template authoring is fiddly; codex-as-gate catches structural template issues. |
| **5** Qwen / VLM / LoRA preprocessing | `holmes` | `standard` | defaults | Several preprocessing surfaces; bounded but each could byte-drift output. |
| **6** Production selector/claim contract | **`all-claude` or `all-codex`** | **`robust`** | `--phase-model plan=claude:xhigh revise=claude:high` | A bad selector schema is a permanent foot-gun. 8 critique checks, max thinking on plan, the schema lives forever. |
| **7** Orchestrator image + pools + artifacts | **`all-claude` or `all-codex`** | `standard` | `--phase-model plan=claude:high` | Pool sizing + artifact TTLs + drain/kill policy. High stakes; standard robustness with high-effort plan is enough. |
| **8** Orchestrated route propagation | **`all-claude` or `all-codex`** | **`robust`** | `--phase-model plan=claude:high revise=claude:high` | The "parent says Comfy, child silently runs WGP" failure mode is exactly what you can't afford. Parent/child consistency edge cases need rigorous critique. |
| **9** Control-rail + travel-matrix parity | `holmes` | `standard` | defaults | Many small parity variants (Canny, Depth, Pose, Flow); bounded per-row. Premium not warranted unless one specific row blows up. |
| **10** Canary readiness integration | `nancy` | `light` | defaults | Dashboards, alerts, runbook prose. |
| **11** Production canary | mixed: `all-claude`/`all-codex` for code patches, `nancy` for runbooks | `standard` for code, `light` for runbooks | high for code | Per-flip changes are operational. Code patches that go in mid-canary need premium because there's no rollback iteration. |
| **12** Dual-executor hardening | `marlowe` | `light` | defaults | Final docs + flip verification. `marlowe` is good at audit-and-gap-fill mode. |
| **12B** Optional cleanup | `nancy` | `light` | defaults | Mechanical PRs after the §8A gate is signed. |

## Two specific things to call out

**Sprint 6 deserves the maximum dial.** The selector schema lives forever — wrong key shape cascades into Sprint 8 and 11. That's why it gets `all-claude`/`all-codex` + `robust` + `claude:xhigh` plan. If you only burn premium budget once in this whole migration, do it here.

**Sprints 2, 6, 7, 8 are the four "don't skimp" sprints.** They define abstractions and contracts that everything else depends on. The other twelve sprints can run cheaper without damaging the migration.

## Rough cost projection

| Tier | Sprints | Per-sprint estimate | Subtotal |
|---|---|---|---|
| `nancy`/light: 0A, 0C, 10, 12B + half of 11 | 4.5 | ~$2 | ~$9 |
| `marlowe`/light: 0B, 3.5, 12 | 3 | ~$3 | ~$9 |
| `marlowe`/standard: 3 | 1 | ~$8 | ~$8 |
| `holmes`/standard: 1, 4, 5, 9 | 4 | ~$30 | ~$120 |
| `all-claude` or `all-codex`/standard: 2, 7 + half of 11 | 2.5 | ~$80 | ~$200 |
| `all-claude` or `all-codex`/robust: 6, 8 | 2 | ~$130 | ~$260 |
| **Total** | **17** | | **~$606** |

Compare to **all-claude/standard everywhere**: 17 × ~$80 = **~$1,360**. Smart triage saves you roughly half the cost while keeping premium quality where it matters (the four contract-defining sprints).

Compare to **all-claude/robust everywhere** (paranoid mode): 17 × ~$130 = **~$2,210**. Smart triage saves ~75%.

If you want, I can stage the megaplan launches one sprint at a time, merging winners into main between sprints — that's the pattern this experiment validated as right (vs. baking all sprints at once where losses compound and you can't isolate which sprint regressed).

Yes — about half a dozen things I used implicitly that aren't in the doc.

**The tacit knowledge:**

1. **A finer deliverable-type taxonomy.** The doc says "verify / routine / medium-stakes / contract." I actually used a more granular mental model when writing the per-sprint table:
   - text/doc → `nancy`
   - mechanical scripts/yaml → `marlowe`/light
   - code with cross-file dependencies → `marlowe`/standard
   - novel code in unfamiliar area → `holmes`
   - contract/schema/wire-format → `all-claude` or `all-codex` + `robust`

   Interpolations between those buckets aren't explicit anywhere.

2. **A single sprint can require multiple profiles.** Sprint 11 has both code patches and runbook updates, so I split the rec by work type. The doc doesn't articulate "if a sprint mixes deliverable types, mix profiles."

3. **Sprint length is uncorrelated with model tier.** The doc has this as a one-line trap. The full corollary I used — *a 3-day contract sprint (Sprint 6 is 2 weeks but the contract decisions are concentrated in days) deserves more than a 2-week mechanical sprint* — isn't drawn out.

4. **Bake-off vs single-arm tradeoff.** I implicitly knew bake-off overhead exceeds value for short discovery sprints (Sprint 0A, 0C, 3.5). The doc doesn't talk about *when to bake-off vs run a single profile*. From the experiment: bake-off is worth it when ≥3 distinct profile mixes are plausible AND the deliverable is a code diff worth comparing AND the per-arm cost is < your decision value.

5. **Sequential migration methodology.** "Stage launches one sprint at a time, merging winners into main between sprints" — I offered this in the per-sprint recs. It came directly from the experiment ("don't bake off all phases as one giant idea — losses compound"). Not in the learnings doc.

6. **Specific failure modes worth watching for.** I treated the codex `worker_blocked` + `awaiting_human` outcomes, the DeepSeek revise mojibake collapse at iter 6, and the brief-driven defects (fabricated SD-9, duplicate hype_smoke.py) as a tacit watchlist when picking profiles. The doc says "brief quality dominates" abstractly but doesn't list "here are the symptoms when a profile is mismatched to the work."

7. **Harness-level caveats that affect outcome interpretation.** Megaplan silently retries revise-on-error and has no critique-loop iteration cap (we discovered both during the experiment). They aren't profile knowledge per se, but they tell you when to distrust an arm's outcome.

8. **The "phases already on main" recognition effect** isn't quite captured as a cost-saver pattern. The doc says "Opus reads repo state better." The mechanism that produces the cost win is more specific: *Opus recognizes already-done work as already-done and exits cheaply, where DeepSeek planners don't.* Worth naming explicitly because it's a cost-saver pattern, not just a quality observation.

**Recommendation:** items 1, 2, 4, 5 are general-purpose enough to belong in the doc — they're decision frameworks that apply beyond this migration. Items 6, 7, 8 are more like field notes; if I add them they'd need to be in a separate "watchlist" section so they don't dilute the core principles. Want me to fold 1-2-4-5 in?

## What changed and why (vs the prior recommendation)

The "slight overkill at boundaries" rule shifted six sprints up one notch:

| Sprint | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| 0B | marlowe + light | marlowe + **standard** (corpus is depended on) |
| 1 | holmes + standard | holmes + **robust** (profiles propagate) |
| 2 | all-claude/codex + standard | all-claude/codex + **robust** (long-lived seam) |
| 3 | marlowe + standard | **holmes** + standard (oracle blocks canary) |
| 7 | all-claude/codex + standard | all-claude/codex + **robust** (no rollback iteration) |
| 11 (code) | all-claude/codex + standard | all-claude/codex + **robust** (mid-canary, no rollback iteration) |
| 12 | marlowe + light | marlowe + **standard** (verification matters) |

Plus three sprints flagged as bake-off candidates (Sprint 2, 6, 8) — these are the long-lived-seam / contract-defining sprints where seeing 3 alternatives produced by different model mixes is worth the extra cost.

Sprint 11 is now explicitly split into two sub-jobs.

## Updated cost projection

| Tier | Sprints | Per-sprint estimate | Subtotal |
|---|---|---|---|
| `nancy`/light: 0A, 0C, 10, 11-runbooks, 12B | 5 | ~$2 | ~$10 |
| `marlowe`/light: 3.5 | 1 | ~$3 | ~$3 |
| `marlowe`/standard: 0B, 12 | 2 | ~$8 | ~$16 |
| `holmes`/standard: 3, 4, 5, 9 | 4 | ~$30 | ~$120 |
| `holmes`/robust: 1 | 1 | ~$50 | ~$50 |
| `all-claude` or `all-codex` /robust: 7, 11-code | 2 | ~$130 | ~$260 |
| Bake-off (3-arm) at all-claude/codex/robust: 2, 6, 8 | 3 | ~$390 | ~$1170 |
| **Total** | **18** | | **~$1,629** |

## Cost comparison

| Strategy | Total |
|---|---|
| **Smart triage (recommended)** | ~$1,630 |
| Smart triage but no bake-offs (single-arm at top tier instead) | ~$850 |
| `all-claude`/`standard` everywhere | ~$1,360 |
| `all-claude`/`robust` everywhere (paranoid mode) | ~$2,210 |

**The bake-off bump from $850 → $1,630 is the price of seeing alternatives on the three most consequential decisions** (adapter shape, selector schema, parent/child propagation). If budget is tight, drop those three to single-arm and you land at ~$850 — still well under the all-claude/standard everywhere baseline, with premium-tier quality concentrated where regressions cascade.

## Operational notes

- **Run sequentially, sprint by sprint.** Merge each winner into main before kicking off the next. Don't batch — losses compound and you can't isolate which sprint regressed.
- **Sprints 2, 6, 8 are the four "don't skimp" sprints** (alongside 7). They define abstractions and contracts that everything else depends on. The other twelve sprints can run cheaper without damaging the migration.
- **For the bake-off sprints (2, 6, 8)**: 3 arms is enough — claude-led, codex-led, and one cross-mix. More than that adds noise, not signal.
- **Sprint 11 mid-canary code patches** should *not* be bake-offs. Bake-off requires worktree isolation and you can't bake-off against live production.

**1. New `poirot` profile** added to user-level config (`~/.config/megaplan/profiles.toml`), mirroring megaplan's built-in `standard`:
- Claude: plan, prep, revise, gate, finalize
- Codex: critique, execute, review

So `--profile poirot` works alongside `--profile standard` — same configuration, more memorable name.

**2. Personality names for `all-claude` and `all-codex`:**
- `all-claude` → **Monk** (Adrian Monk — solo virtuoso obsessed with thoroughness)
- `all-codex` → **Columbo** (Lt. Columbo — solo analyst, "just one more thing")

The practical names stay (so you still type `--profile all-claude`), but the personality monikers are present in the doc so they fit the same shorthand format as the others.

**3. Dash-shorthand consistency** — every row in the profile table now follows the format:

> **`name`** *(detective — personality)* — model-A phaseX/phaseY — model-B phaseZ — ...

For example:
- nancy → DeepSeek plan/revise/finalize/execute — codex:medium prep/critique/gate/review
- holmes → Opus:medium plan/revise — codex:medium gate/review — Kimi K2.6 critique — DeepSeek prep/finalize/execute
- poirot → Claude plan/prep/revise/gate/finalize — codex critique/execute/review

**4. Promoted poirot** in the deliverable-type table for the contract/schema/wire-format row (top tier), with `all-claude`/`all-codex` as fallback.

**5. Added a `poirot + robust` row** to the combinations table — apex for the toughest tasks.

The doc now has one consistent format for all six profiles (nancy, marlowe, holmes, all-claude/Monk, all-codex/Columbo, poirot), with `poirot` positioned as the top tier for tasks demanding both premiums.

> DEVELOPER

Are they secondary names or what's the best way to-

> AGENT

There are basically three sane options. My take on each:

**1. Aliases** (what I did with `poirot` — separate profile entries that mirror the original).
- Pro: `--profile monk` works.
- Con: same config has two names (mental overhead). Drift risk if config changes — you'd have to update both.

**2. Doc-only nicknames** (what I currently have for `all-claude`/`all-codex` — practical name in TOML, personality name only in the doc).
- Pro: TOML stays the source of truth. No drift.
- Con: can't type `--profile monk` — you have to type `all-claude`.

**3. Personality as the primary name with the practical name as alias.**
- Pro: forces personality use, more memorable in CLI.
- Con: breaks muscle memory; `all-claude` is a perfectly good name and people already know what it does.

**My recommendation: keep them doc-only nicknames** for `all-claude`/`all-codex` (option 2). Reasoning:

- `poirot` deserved the alias because `standard` is genuinely a misleading name (it's not "standard" in any common sense — it's a specific Claude+codex mix).
- `all-claude` and `all-codex` are *self-describing* — the practical name already tells you exactly what it does. Adding `monk`/`columbo` as aliases gives you nothing functional, and you'd have two TOML entries pointing at the same config.
- The doc already gets the personality framing across. Anyone reading the table knows `all-claude` is Monk and `all-codex` is Columbo. They can still type `--profile all-claude`.

So nothing to change in the TOML for monk/columbo — they're already labelled in the doc and that's enough. `poirot` stays as an alias because `standard` is the misleading one. Want me to leave it that way, or do you want monk/columbo as actual `--profile`-able aliases too?

| **7** Orchestrator image + pools + artifacts | `all-claude` *or* `all-codex` | `standard` | `plan=claude:high` | No | Pool sizing + drain/kill policy. Single-model uniformity matters more than dual-perspective here. |

| ↳ Code patches | **`poirot`** | `standard` | `plan=claude:high` | No | Mid-canary patches have no rollback iteration. |
| ↳ Runbook + dashboard updates | `nancy` | `light` | defaults | No | Don't pay premium for the runbooks. |

## What changed vs the prior recommendation

| Sprint | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | holmes / **robust** / plan=high | holmes / **standard** / plan=high |
| 2 | all-claude·codex / **robust** / plan=high revise=high | **poirot** / standard / plan=high revise=high |
| 6 | all-claude·codex / **robust** / plan=xhigh revise=high | **poirot** / standard / plan=xhigh revise=high |
| 7 | all-claude·codex / **robust** / plan=high | all-claude·codex / **standard** / plan=high |
| 8 | all-claude·codex / **robust** / plan=high revise=high | **poirot** / standard / plan=high revise=high |
| 11 code | all-claude·codex / **robust** / plan=high | **poirot** / standard / plan=high |

Robust is gone everywhere. Sprints 2, 6, 8, 11-code that previously bumped to robust now use `poirot` (both premiums) at standard with thinking pushed up. The asymmetry (high/xhigh planner with default-low critic) does the work that robust would have done, without paying for 4 extra critique cycles.

## Cost projection

| Tier | Sprints | Per-sprint estimate | Subtotal |
|---|---|---|---|
| `nancy`/light: 0A, 0C, 10, 11-runbooks, 12B | 5 | ~$2 | ~$10 |
| `marlowe`/light: 3.5 | 1 | ~$3 | ~$3 |
| `marlowe`/standard: 0B, 12 | 2 | ~$8 | ~$16 |
| `holmes`/standard +high plan: 1, 3, 4, 5, 9 | 5 | ~$35 | ~$175 |
| `all-claude` or `all-codex`/standard: 7 | 1 | ~$100 | ~$100 |
| `poirot`/standard with high thinking: 11-code | 1 | ~$80 | ~$80 |
| Bake-offs (3-arm) at `poirot`/standard with high/xhigh thinking: 2, 6, 8 | 3 | ~$270-330 | ~$880 |
| **Total** | **18** | | **~$1,265** |

## Cost comparison

| Strategy | Total |
|---|---|
| **Smart triage, no robust, max thinking, with bake-offs** *(this rec)* | ~$1,265 |
| Same but no bake-offs (single-arm at top tier instead) | ~$670 |
| Prior rec (with robust + bake-offs) | ~$1,630 |
| `all-claude` / `standard` everywhere | ~$1,360 |
| `all-claude` / `robust` everywhere (paranoid) | ~$2,210 |

Dropping robust + pushing thinking saves ~$365 vs the prior rec and stays well under all-claude-everywhere. Without bake-offs, you land at ~$670 — half the all-claude/standard baseline.

## When would I still consider `robust`?

Strict reading of the doc principle says reserve it for when *the critic surface is genuinely unbounded* — i.e., the plan touches so much surface area that 4 critique checks plausibly miss something. None of these 18 sprints clearly hit that bar; all of them have bounded scope. So `robust` doesn't appear anywhere in this rec. If you ever want to bring it back, Sprint 6 is the strongest candidate (selector schema, downstream cascades) — but only if `poirot/standard + plan=claude:xhigh` doesn't catch what you need. Push thinking first, escalate to robust last.
